Attorneys Ben Crump and Bob Hilliard File Lawsuits on Behalf of Amazon Workers, Victims of Amazon Warehouse Collapse During Deadly Tornadoes
============================================================================================================================================

[Home](https://bencrump.com/) » [Press](https://bencrump.com/press/) » Attorneys Ben Crump and Bob Hilliard File Lawsuits on Behalf of Amazon Workers, Victims of Amazon Warehouse Collapse During Deadly Tornadoes

**Read filed court documents:**

1.  [Amazon Warehouse Complaint- WD-FINAL.pdf](https://bencrump.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/Amazon-Warehouse-Complaint-WD-FINAL.pdf)
2.  [Amazon Warehouse PTSD Complaint FINAL.pdf](https://bencrump.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/Amazon-Warehouse-PTSD-Complaint-FINAL.pdf)

**  
EDWARDSVILLE, Ill.––** Renowned civil rights attorneys Ben Crump of Ben Crump Law, Bob Hilliard of Hilliard Martinez Gonzales, and attorneys Patrick King and William Miller of MillerKing Law Firm announced today that they have filed two lawsuits on behalf of victims of the deadly Amazon warehouse collapse that occurred on Dec. 10, 2021, when tornadoes touched down in Edwardsville. Plaintiffs include Deon January, mother and the administrator for the estate of DeAndre Morrow, who was killed in the collapse, and Amazon drivers Jamarco Hickman, Evan Jensen, Jada Williams, and Deontae Yancey who survived the collapse but suffered physical or mental harm as a result of Amazon’s negligence.

On Dec. 10, 2021, Mr. Morrow and the other plaintiffs were delivering packages for Amazon out of the company’s Edwardsville, Illinois, fulfillment center. Amazon was warned by the National Weather Service of possible tornadoes in the area of the warehouse as far as 36 hours ahead of the tragic warehouse collapse.

As stated in the complaints, upon receipt of the tornado warnings, Amazon allegedly did not modify the employee work schedule and refused to allow employees from taking time off until the storm passed. In fact, Mr. Morrow was scheduled to take his scheduled day off but was called from dispatch at 9:12 a.m., asking him to work an extra shift. Mr. Morrow was working extra shifts and overtime in order to earn extra money for the holiday season and to repay his mother for a car that she had recently purchased for him. Mr. Morrow’s shift was scheduled between 9:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. but he was present at the facility long after his shift was scheduled to end.

Prior to the tornado hitting the facility, plaintiffs Evan Jensen, Jada Williams, and Deontae Yancey all attempted to leave the facility and seek shelter at home but were threatened with termination by Amazon management. A little while later, Amazon received additional tornado warnings between 8:06 p.m. and 8:16 p.m. They responded by warning only a portion of the employees and instructing them to retreat into the warehouse restrooms for safety. The victims were all located at the warehouse against their will when a tornado hit the building at approximately 8:20 pm. The center’s walls collapsed resulting in numerous injuries and the death of six individuals, including DeAndre Morrow. Mr. Morrow died as a result of his thoracic cavity being crushed by the Amazon walls around him.

“Amazon had numerous warnings and opportunities to put their employees’ safety first, but they chose their bottom line instead,” said Crump. “As a result, six people needlessly lost their lives and many others suffered injury and mental anguish that will likely last a lifetime. Amazon required their employees to work just moments before the tornado destroyed the fulfillment center, despite their pleas to seek shelter at home with their loved ones. It was Amazon’s responsibility to ensure the safety of their workers and they failed in every respect.”

A West County EMA & Fire Protection District’s Report authored by Dan Bruno stated “…I found what I believed to be one or more significant structural issues with the Amazon building that may have contributed to the failure of the structure.”

As alleged in the complaint, the additional failures of Amazon to protect its employees is extensive and includes:

1.  Failing to warn about or mitigate known safety risks and hazards;
2.  Failing to have a basement shelter or actual shelter;
3.  Failing to implement proper safety procedures in the event of an evacuation or natural disaster and follow procedures while the natural disaster was unfolding;
4.  Failing to properly monitor inclement weather prior to the tornado hitting the fulfillment center;
5.  Failing to operate, maintain, and manage a warehouse in an area prone to tornadoes that was built to withstand tornado size gusts;
6.  Failing to provide a safe room and ensure that employees were in the safest place in the fulfillment center when the tornado touched ground;
7.  Requiring employees to continue working until the moments before the tornado struck when Amazon knew or should have known the tornado was imminent;
8.  Failing to timely inform individuals at the subject fulfillment center that a tornado was approaching so those individuals had adequate time to properly shelter or evacuate; and
9.  Failing to evacuate all those present at the subject delivery station when Amazon knew or should have known that keeping individuals working at the center, including DeAndre Morrow, placed them in imminent danger when Amazon knew or should have known the area was at risk of a tornado.

“Amazon’s documented history of choosing the almighty dollar over the health and safety of their employees must come to an end,” said Hilliard. “They must be held accountable for this deadly and preventable tragedy that took the lives of six Amazon employees and harmed others for life. It was because of Amazon’s negligence and shameful priority of profit that DeAndre Morrow suffered a tragic and needless death, and Mr. Hickman, Mr. Jensen, Ms. Williams, and Mr. Yancey sustained life-altering trauma.”

**IN THE CIRCUIT COURT**

**FOR THE THIRD JUDICIAL CIRCUIT**


**MADISON COUNTY, ILLINOIS**


**JAMARCO HICKMAN, EVAN JENSEN,** )
**JADA WILLIAMS, and** **)**
**DEONTAE YANCEY** )
)
**Plaintiffs,** ) Case No. 22-L)
vs. )
)
**AMAZON.COM, INC** ., a corporation, )
**AMAZON LOGISTICS, INC.**, a corporation )
**CONTEGRA CONSTRUCTION COMPANY**, )
**LLC**, a limited liability company, )
**TRISTAR PROPERTIES, LLC,** a limited )
liability company, **)**
**STOCK & ASSOCIATES CONSULTING** )
**ENGINEERS, INC** ., a corporation, )
**GRAY DESIGN GROUP, INC.**, )
a corporation, and )
**MCNEALY ENGINEERING, INC.**, )
a corporation. )
)
**Defendants** . )


**PLAINTIFFS’ ORIGINAL COMPLAINT**


Plaintiffs, JAMARCO HICKMAN, EVAN JENSEN, JADA WILLIAMS, and


DEONTAE YANCEY (collectively “Plaintiffs”) in the above-entitled cause through their


attorneys, MILLER KING LAW FIRM, HILLIARD MARTINEZ GONZALES LLP, and BEN


CRUMP LAW PLLC against the following Defendants, AMAZON.COM, INC. (“AMAZON


INC.”), AMAZON LOGISTICS, INC (“ALI”), CONTEGRA CONSTRUCTION COMPANY,


LLC (“CONTEGRA”), TRISTAR PROPERTIES, LLC (“TRISTAR”), STOCK &


ASSOCIATES CONSULTING ENGINEERS, INC. (“STOCK”), GRAY DESIGN GROUP, INC.


(“GRAY”), and MCNEALY ENGINEERING, INC. (“MCNEALY”), and shows unto this


Honorable Court as follows:


**I.**

**PLAINTIFFS**


1. Plaintiff, Jamarco Hickman, is an individual who resides in Godfrey, Madison


County, Illinois. Plaintiff may be reached through the undersigned counsel.


2. Plaintiff, Evan Jensen, is an individual who resides in Alton, Madison County,


Illinois. Plaintiff may be reached through the undersigned counsel.


3. Plaintiff, Deontae Yancey, is an individual who resides in Godfrey, Madison


County, Illinois. Plaintiff may be reached through the undersigned counsel.


4. Plaintiff, Jada Williams, is an individual who resides in Glen Carbon, Madison


County, Illinois. Plaintiff may be reached through the undersigned counsel.


**II.**

**DEFENDANTS**


5. Defendant, AMAZON.COM, INC., is a Fortune 100 company headquartered in


Seattle, Washington. Defendant, AMAZON.COM, INC., and its subsidiaries (“AMAZON”,


“AMAZON FLEX”, “AMAZON.COM, LLC”, and Defendant, ALI) comprise the world’s


largest retailer.


6. In 2019, Amazon caused over 2.5 billion packages to be delivered throughout the


United States, including in Illinois. It is estimated that by the end of 2022, Amazon’s package


delivery volume could reach 6.5 billion packages per year in the United States.


7. Defendant, AMAZON.COM, INC., maintains, manages, and controls over 100


“fulfillment centers” and/or “delivery stations” in the United States. These “fulfillment centers”


and/or “delivery stations” are used to store, ship, and deliver goods that customers order through


the Amazon website, thereby creating a vast network by which Defendant, AMAZON, INC., can


provide the ordered goods to customers.


2


8. On December 10, 2021, and at all relevant times, Defendant, AMAZON INC.,


operated, maintained, controlled, and managed through its employees and/or agents a warehouse


or “delivery station” known as “DLI4” located in Edwardsville, Illinois.


9. In addition, on December 10, 2021, and at all relevant times, Defendant,


AMAZON INC., and AMAZON LOGISTICS, used a wide range of independently contracted


drivers and delivery carriers known as Delivery Service Partners (“DSPs”) to drive, haul, and


make deliveries for Defendants, AMAZON INC., and ALI.


10. The DSP program was carefully designed to allow Amazon and ALI to shift costs


and liabilities onto DSPs, while maintaining complete control over the DSPs’ day-to-day


operations, drivers, and potential for success. On information and belief, Amazon designed and


implemented the DSP program for the primary purpose of improperly evading employment laws,


labor and wage laws, transportation and logistics laws and regulations, motor vehicle negligence


liability exposure, and other legal responsibility arising from control over a vast army of delivery


drivers and massive fleet of delivery vans.


11. Namely, Amazon sought to interpose a layer of supposedly “independent”


business entities, DSPs, between itself and its drivers to act as a legal firewall between Amazon


and its employees. In reality, the DSPs themselves served as Amazon’s managerial employees


that hired and managed Amazon’s delivery drivers and ran Amazon’s delivery operations.


Through this sleight-of-hand, Amazon sought to disguise and deny employing and controlling


the operations of tens of thousands of delivery drivers while shifting all operational liability onto


hundreds of DSPs yet ensuring that Amazon, and not DSPs, would capture all the value created


by the DSPs and its other contractors’ hard work and labor.


12. Defendants, AMAZON.COM, INC. and AMAZON LOGISTICS, INC., will be


3


collectively referred to as Defendant AMAZON.


13. Defendant, CONTEGRA, is headquartered in Edwardsville, Illinois and maintains


members that are domiciled in Illinois. Defendant, CONTEGRA, is a construction and


development company that builds commercial retail buildings, warehouses, office buildings, and


institutions. Defendant, CONTEGRA, built, developed, and/or constructed DLI4. Defendant,


CONTEGRA, was under contract with Defendants, AMAZON INC., AMAZON LOGISTICS,


and/or TRISTAR, to build, develop and/or construct the subject warehouse.


14. Defendant, TRISTAR, is headquartered in Missouri. Defendant, TRISTAR, is a


developer, redeveloper, and real estate acquirer of industrial real estate. Defendant, TRISTAR,


was the developer of DLI4. Defendant, TRISTAR, was under contract with Defendants,


AMAZON INC., AMAZON LOGISTICS and/or CONTEGRA, to build, develop and/or


construct the subject warehouse located in Edwardsville, Illinois.


15. Defendant, STOCK, is a civil engineering and land surveying firm based in St.


Louis, Missouri. Defendant, STOCK, provided construction specifications, shop drawings, and


engineering specifications for the build of DLI4, including but not limited to construction


specifications, shop drawings, and engineering specifications to build the facility in a “tilt-up”


manner.


16. Defendant, GRAY, is headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri. Defendant GRAY


provides specialized design services, architectural, engineering, and related services. Defendant,


GRAY, joined Defendants, AMAZON.COM, INC., TRISTAR, CONTEGRA, and STOCK as the


master planning, design, and architectural firm for DLI4. Defendant, GRAY, was under contract


with Defendants, AMAZON.COM, INC., AMAZON LOGISTICS, INC., CONTEGRA,


TRISTAR, and/or STOCK, to design, develop, and/or construct the subject warehouse located in


4


Edwardsville, Illinois.


17. Defendant, MCNEALY ENGINEERING, INC., is a structural engineering firm


based in St. Louis, Missouri that provides architectural restoration, structural engineering, and


architectural engineering services including such services for the DLI4.


**III.**

**JURISDICTION AND VENUE**


18. This Court has jurisdiction over all of the parties and the subject matter involved


in this litigation as the amount in controversy exceeds the Court’s jurisdictional minimum


requirements.


19. Venue is proper in Madison County, Illinois because the incident giving rise to


this suit occurred in this County, pursuant to 735 ILCS 5/2-101.


20. Jurisdiction is proper in this Court over all Defendants as Defendants reside in or


conduct continuous and systematic business in the State of Illinois. Plaintiff expressly disavows


that any claims are being made pursuant to federal law, treaties, or constitution.


**21.** Although the amount in controversy exceeds $50,000.00, exclusive of costs and


interest, there is a lack of complete diversity because of the presence of a Plaintiff and one or


more of Defendants that are citizens of Illinois. As such, this case is not removable to Federal


Court. Any removal would be improper and should be remedied by sanctions and a remand with


an award of all costs, expenses, and fees including, but not limited to, attorney fees under 28


U.S.C. § 1447(c).


**IV.**

**FACTS**


**A.** **A Deadly And Destructive Tornado Strikes Amazon’s DLI4 Fulfillment**
**Center.**


1. On or about December 10, 2021, each Plaintiff was delivery driver for a DSP who


5


provided delivery services for Amazon. Plaintiffs’ delivery work was based out of Amazon’s


“DLI4” fulfillment center in Edwardsville, Illinois, delivering packages. As noted above,


Defendant Amazon is the owner, operator, and employer for the warehouse, and assumed the


duty and responsibility for ensuring safe operations for its employees.


2. That day, at approximately 8:20 p.m., an EF-3 tornado began on the south side of


Interstate 270 and moved northeast, striking DLI4, causing parts of the center’s walls to collapse


and other multiple structure failures. Each Plaintiff was physically located at DLI4 when the


subject EF-3 tornado hit the warehouse and endured the destruction that the tornado unleashed at


the warehouse. Pivotally, as detailed below, each Plaintiff was physically located at the DLI4


Amazon fulfillment center during the tornado against their will.


3. Importantly, Defendant Amazon was warned by the National Weather Service of


possible tornadoes in the area of the warehouse as far as thirty-six (36) hours ahead of this tragic


incident. Upon receipt of these warnings, Defendant Amazon allegedly did not modify the


employee or contractor work schedule and refused to permit employees from taking time off


until the storm passed. On or about December 10, 2021, Defendant Amazon received additional


tornado warnings between 8:06 p.m. and 8:16 p.m. Defendant Amazon inadequately responded


by warning only a portion of the employees and instructing them to retreat into the warehouse


restrooms for safety. The tornado hit at roughly 8:26 p.m. that evening with 150 m.p.h. winds


which ripped off the roof of the warehouse and caused 11-inch-thick concrete walls to fall in on


themselves.


4. Tragically, due to Defendant Amazon’s blatant disregard for its employees’ and


contractors’ safety and well-being and motivated by profit and productivity at the expense of its


workers’ health, as well as the negligent and willful acts or omissions of Defendants


6


CONTEGRA, TRISTAR, STOCK, GRAY, and MCNEALY in building, developing, designing,


creating specifications for, and/constructing DLI4, numerous people were injured and at least six


(6) people lost their lives when the EF-3 tornado struck DLI4 on December 10, 2021. This


horrible tragedy was preventable, had basic and necessary care and concern for Defendant


Amazon’s workers been applied by Defendant Amazon, as it were legally obligated to do.


5. Unfortunately, this incident is only the latest in a pattern of Amazon disregarding


employee safety and ignoring warnings of oncoming natural disasters.


 - On or about September 2021, similar warehouses ran by Defendant Amazon ignored


similar warnings by the National Weather Service of the oncoming tropical depression


“Ida” which led to the deaths of fourteen (14) employees.


 - In 2021, when warned of widespread record-breaking high heatwaves over the summer of


that year, Defendant Amazon refused to take adequate measures which led to the


widespread employee health issues and the death of an employee within a similar


warehouse in Bessemer, Alabama.


 - On or about November 8, 2018, Defendant Amazon ignored warnings as a result of a


wildfire in California putting their employees at risk in the name of productivity and


profits.


 - In November 2018, Defendant Amazon had another warehouse that was struck by a


tornado in Baltimore, Maryland, that caused the warehouse to collapse and two (2) men


to die as a result.


**B.** **Amazon’s Control Over DSP Drivers Like Plaintiffs**


6. Amazon’s failure to protect Plaintiffs and others at the DLI4 fulfillment center is


magnified by the extent of control which Amazon exhibited over Plaintiffs’ work. Indeed,


7


Amazon closely monitored all materials aspects of Plaintiffs’ work and controlled, directed,


and/or instructed Plaintiffs on the operative details of their work, including but not limited to,


controlling the deliveries and the routes Plaintiffs followed. Illustrative examples of the extent of


Amazon’s control over Plaintiffs’ work include but are not limited to the below.


7. Defendant Amazon required Plaintiffs to wear a uniform and/or apparel that


displayed the name “Amazon” on it. Defendant Amazon provided DSP drivers with a $120 store


credit to Zappos.com to purchase work shoes.


8. The nature of the work performed by drivers was similar and standardized at each


Amazon delivery station and was centrally controlled and directed by Amazon.


9. Plaintiffs were also required to follow the policies and procedures of Defendant


Amazon, controlling the number of deliveries Plaintiffs made during a shift, monitoring and scoring work


performance, requiring Plaintiffs to share phone data, and having the means to terminate the employment


of Plaintiffs.


10. Amazon controlled the drivers’ day-to-day activities through direct contact with


them.


11. Amazon set the delivery routes and then assigned and provided them to its DSPs.


Every week, Amazon sent the DSPs the number, type, and start time for the delivery routes for


the upcoming week.


12. DSP drivers were each assigned a cell phone loaded with proprietary Amazon


delivery software (“Amazon Flex”) and drove an Amazon-branded vehicle to the Amazon


delivery station, where Amazon employees pre-sorted packages for delivery. Drivers then logged


into Amazon Flex to access their Amazon assigned route and picked up the assigned packages.


The packages were not transformed or modified during the shipping process but were delivered


8


in the same condition as they were shipped to the Amazon delivery station.


13. Amazon, through a proprietary system called Cortex, tracked, and monitored the


DSP drivers’ job performance in real time, tracking delivery rate, delivery speed, delivery


accuracy, driver distractions, seatbelt use, driving speed and acceleration, and adherence to a


delivery schedule created by Amazon through Amazon Flex and its EMentor application. Every


day, Amazon sent an email to the DSPs documenting each delivery driver’s job performance.


14. Amazon required DSP drivers to explain why any package was returned to the


station at the end of a driver’s shift. Amazon routinely threatened drivers with suspension or


termination if they did not go back out to attempt redelivery of 100% of dispatched packages,


even if the driver had been on the road more than ten hours.


15. Amazon set the start time and end time for drivers and dictated the hours of


delivery in which a delivery driver could deliver a package, including the start time and end time


for each route. For example, Amazon employees sent delivery drivers text messages when they


approached ten hours of work.


16. Amazon employees also direct DSP employees to cease delivering or to continue


delivering. On more than one occasion, DSP drivers were called back to the delivery station and


told not to deliver packages well before the drivers’ shifts had ended.


**C.** **Plaintiffs At DLI4 Against Their Will When Storm Hits.**


17. Plaintiff Evan Jensen was employed by XSeed, Inc., an Amazon DSP contractor,


for approximately six months prior to the tornado. Plaintiff Jensen was provided an Amazon


truck equipped with a 4-way camera and an Amazon uniform. On December 10, 2021, Mr.


Jensen’s shift was scheduled between 9:00 a.m. and 8:30 p.m.


18. At approximately 7:00 p.m., Mr. Jensen sent a text message to his manager


9


requesting to return to the warehouse. Following such approval, Mr. Jensen arrived at DLI4 at


approximately 8:00 p.m. Mr. Jensen attempted to leave the warehouse to return home before the


storm hit but was threatened with termination by a warehouse official if he left the warehouse.


The storm hit around 8:30 p.m.


19. Fearful of termination, Mr. Jensen remained in the warehouse and was directed to


take shelter in the warehouse break room at the time of the storm. Upon information and belief,


Plaintiff Jenson believes he would have made it to his personal residence if he would have been


allowed to leave the warehouse when he first texted his manager around 7:00 p.m.


20. Plaintiff Jada Williams was employed by XSeed, Inc., an Amazon DSP


contractor, for approximately two weeks prior to the tornado. Plaintiff Williams was provided an


Amazon truck equipped with a 4-way camera and an Amazon uniform. On December 10, 2021,


Ms. Williams’ shift was scheduled between 9:00 a.m. and 8:30 p.m.


21. Ms. Williams was directed to take shelter in a bathroom on the north end of the


warehouse at the time of the storm. Ms. Williams attempted to leave the warehouse to return


home before the storm hit but was threatened with termination by a warehouse official if she left


the warehouse.


22. Plaintiff Deontae Yancey was employed by XSeed, Inc., an Amazon DSP


contractor, for approximately three months prior to the tornado. Plaintiff was provided an


Amazon truck equipped with a 4-way camera and an Amazon uniform. On December 10, 2021,


Ms. Williams’ shift was scheduled between 10:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.


23. Defendant Amazon would require its drivers to “rescue” fellow drivers when


other drivers had not completed their scheduled deliveries. To “rescue” another driver means to


go out and help them finish delivering their packages.


10


24. National Weather Service alerts covering St. Louis County and Madison County,


including Edwardsville, were issued via Twitter at 6:17 p.m.:

![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11463689475448474597/11463689475448474597.pdf-10-0.png)


25. At 6:32 p.m., Mr. Yancey was nearly finished with his delivery route when he


received a message from Nikita Sunil via the Amazon Flex App requesting that he rescue a


fellow driver.


11


![](https://wy-static.wenxiaobai.com/11463689475448474597/11463689475448474597.pdf-11-0.png)

26. Fearful of the approaching storm, Mr. Yancey refused to participate in the rescue.


27. When Mr. Yancey returned to the warehouse, he was directed to take shelter in a


bathroom on the north end of the warehouse at the time of the storm. Mr. Yancey attempted to


leave the warehouse to return home before the storm, however, he was told to “stay put and not


to leave” by warehouse officials.


28. Plaintiff Jamarco Hickman was employed by ABC & DAD, Inc., an Amazon DSP


contractor, for approximately four months prior to the collapse of the warehouse. Plaintiff


Hickman was provided an Amazon truck equipped with a 4-way camera and an Amazon


uniform. On December 10, 2021, Mr. Hickman’s shift was scheduled between 9:30 a.m. and 8:30


p.m.


29. On Thursday, December 9, 2021, a team huddle was conducted in the warehouse


staging area inside of the delivery garage wherein the dispatch manager announced that Amazon


wanted more drivers on the road because of the holiday peak season so drivers were expected to


begin normally scheduled shifts one hour earlier than their scheduled shift. During this meeting,


the dispatcher manager also announced a peak season incentive program, wherein drivers could


earn a $20 Amazon gift card for delivering 200 additional packages per day.


12


30. On December 10, 2021, at approximately 7:40 p.m., Mr. Hickman finished a


rescue of a fellow driver. He called dispatch and requested permission to return to the warehouse


to turn in his truck and complete his shift. He noticed the sky was becoming increasingly dark so


he hurriedly returned to the warehouse so that he could gather his belongings and return home.


31. Mr. Hickman returned to the DLI4 warehouse at approximately 8:15 p.m. He was


immediately instructed to park his delivery van and go to the restrooms for shelter where he


remained until emergency medical services arrived following the storm.


32. On and before December 10, 2021, Defendant Amazon employed an individual


and/or individuals at the subject Amazon fulfillment center that were responsible for monitoring


severe weather updates.


33. On December 10, 2021, Defendant Amazon, knew or should have known that


tornadoes were possible at or near the subject “fulfillment center” as early as 3:44 a.m. on


Thursday, December 9, 2021, when the National Weather Service issued the following weather


warning: “ _There is chance of thunderstorms late Friday afternoon into the night across_


_southeastern and east-central Missouri as well as south-central and southwestern Illinois. A few_


_thunderstorms could become strong to severe in southeastern Missouri and southwestern Illinois_


_late Friday evening into night. The main threat will be strong to damage wind gusts, but a_


_tornado is also possible._ ”


34. On December 10, 2021, Defendant Amazon, again knew or should have known


that tornadoes were possible at or near the subject “fulfillment center” when the National


Weather Service on December 9, 2021 at 2:58 p.m. reported: “ _Scattered severe storms are_


_possible across southeast Missouri and southwest Illinois between 8:00 p.m. Friday night and_


_3:00 a.m. early Saturday. Any storms that develop will be fast moving. The primary threat with_


13


_these storms will be damaging winds. A few tornadoes will be possible as well._ ”


**D.** **Amazon’s Knowledge Of The Tornado And Its Severity.**


35. On December 10, 2021 at 8:06 p.m., the National Weather Service issued a “take


shelter now” tornado warning for the Edwardsville, Illinois area.


36. Despite having numerous warnings from the National Weather Service that the


Edwardsville, Illinois area was at risk of experiencing devastating weather and/or tornadoes,


Defendant Amazon had workers and independently contracted Delivery Service Partners


(“DSP”) working during a holiday “peak season” until moments before the EF-3’s tornado


obliterated the subject fulfillment center in Edwardsville, Illinois.


37. At all times on December 10, 2021, Defendant Amazon, knew or should have


known and foreseen that the subject fulfillment center was in an area that could sustain


devastating weather and/or a tornado.


38. On December 10, 2021 and at all relevant times, Defendant Amazon, had duties


to exercise reasonable care in its operation, management, and/or control of the subject fulfillment


center and all workers present at the center, including but not limited to, independently


contracted DSP contractors including Plaintiffs, to prevent them from sustaining injuries and


death.


39. Plaintiffs attach as “Exhibit A” to this Complaint the West County EMA & Fire


Protection District’s Report authored by Dan Bruno, P.E., PTOE, to further support Plaintiffs’


causes of action against Defendants.


40. As stated by Mr. Bruno, “…I found what I believed to be one or more significant


structural issues with the Amazon building that may have contributed to the failure of the


structure.” _See_ Exhibit A at 4. Shockingly, Mr. Bruno discovered why these columns failed and


14


caused the death of these six (6) individuals:


“In each case of the failed columns, there was a clear line of demarcation on the
bottom of the column just below the yellow band that showed an area of
unpainted column with light brown surface oxidation that had been the area of the
column that sat below the finished grade of the concrete floor. I became
concerned when I noticed that none of the columns appeared to be ripped or torn
from the base. This was especially concerning to me knowing that the
International Building Code (IBC) requires structural members to be secured
against uplift from wind loads, among other things. (2021 IBC Section 1604.8.1).
Looking at the base of the columns more closely, I could find no weld or bolted
connection at the base of any column, but only a bead of what appeared to be
some sort of caulk around the column at the finished floor line. An examination of
several of the empty pockets where [sic] columns once stood also did not reveal
any indication of positive securement of the column et at or below the finished
floor level.”


_See_ Exhibit A at 2.


41. As a result of Defendants’ negligence and continuous blatant disregard for the


health and safety of their workers, Plaintiffs suffered life-altering injuries and damages.


**COUNTS**

34.content:
Lucy HookerBusiness reporter, New York

Watch drone footage of the Amazon warehouse in Illinois after its roof collapsed

**Amazon is facing questions over health and safety policies at a warehouse in the US state of Illinois after six workers died when the building was destroyed by a tornado.**

"This never would have happened if they cared about lives over productivity," the sister of one of the victims commented on social media.

The company says its team had "worked quickly" in response to the tornado.

The roof collapsed as the storm hit the warehouse on Friday.

Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson, said in a statement the company is "deeply saddened" by the deaths.

One of those who died, Clayton Cope, 29, spoke to his family on the phone shortly before the building in the town of Edwardsville, Illinois was struck.

Clayton's mother Carla, said she had called her son to warn him of the tornado's approach.

"We told him it looked like the storm was heading that way and that he needed to get to shelter," Carla told NBC affiliated television station KSDK.

Clayton, who had previously trained in the Navy, told his mother he would first warn his co-workers.

![Image 1](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20251210-151139-37baf2dfdd-web-2.36.1-1/grey-placeholder.png)![Image 2: Cope family Clayton Cope on a motorbike](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/3CF8/production/_122080651_265073477_4442528092513134_6196711549804121836_n.jpg.webp)Cope family

Clayton Cope told his family he wanted to warn other workers before seeking shelter himself

Now, questions are being raised over whether adequate shelter was available, whether workers were advised to go there immediately, and whether the shifts should have gone ahead that evening at all, given the warnings of severe weather.

The Edwardsville site received tornado warnings between 20:06 and 20:16 local time (01:06 and 01:16 GMT) before the tornado struck the building at 20:27, Amazon said in a statement when contacted by the BBC, with events "happening incredibly fast".

The company said that the team worked "incredibly quickly" to ensure as many employees and partners could reach the "shelter in place" site.

One cargo driver, Austin J McEwen, 26, died in the bathroom, where many workers said they had been directed to shelter after receiving emergency alerts on their mobile phones.

"I was just getting in the building and they started screaming, "Shelter in place!'" said David Kosiak, 26, who has worked at the facility for three months. "We were in the bathrooms. That's where they sent us."

"It sounded like a train came through the building. The ceiling tiles came flying down. It was very loud. They made us shelter in place until we left - it was at least two-and-a-half hours in there," Mr Kosiak said.

Amazon said following a tornado warning company procedure was for all employees to be "notified and directed to move to a designated and marked shelter in place location".

The majority of the team had taken shelter at "the primary designated location", the firm said, but a small group had taken shelter in a part of the building that was hit by the tornado. "This is where most of the tragic loss of life occurred," Amazon said.

But Clayton's sister Rachel told the BBC that she understood from the conversation between her brother and her parents that he and the other workers were not immediately told to shelter after the first warning siren sounded.

She posted an comment on Facebook calling for publicity around the firm's approach to health and safety.

"Everyone knows that all Amazon cares about is productivity," she wrote.

She said she didn't believe her brother would have died if the company "got them \[the employees\] to safety after the storm started to get bad and took it seriously".

"No-one would have been frantically getting to the shelter last minute and my brother wouldn't have had to help people get to the shelter and put his life at risk," she wrote.

"I want them to answer for this, I want this to be a starting point of places taking the lives of their employees seriously and treating them as more than a number."

The deadly storms swept through six US states on Friday evening causing the deaths of almost 100 people and damaging homes and businesses over a 200 mile (322 km) area. In Mayfield, Kentucky eight deaths were confirmed at a candle factory.

The National Weather Service said the storm had intensified rapidly as it struck the Amazon warehouse with winds peaking at 150 miles per hour (241 km-per-hour), ripping the roof off the football field-sized structure. The 11-inch (28-cm) thick concrete walls fell in on themselves.

Stuart Appelbaum, president of the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union, which is trying to unionise Amazon workers in different parts of the US, said it was "inexcusable" that the company required people to work despite the tornado warning.

On Monday, US Department of Labor said an investigation into the building collapse has been opened by the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

![Image 3](https://static.files.bbci.co.uk/bbcdotcom/web/20251210-151139-37baf2dfdd-web-2.36.1-1/grey-placeholder.png)![Image 4: Getty Images Amazon warehouse damaged in tornado](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/D938/production/_122080655_gettyimages-1237190053.jpg.webp)Getty Images

The roof of the building buckled as the tornado hit

Rebecca Givan, associate professor at Rutgers University's School of Management and Labour Relations, said companies have a legal requirement to maintain a safe workplace but the penalties for violating it are very weak.

From an ethical standpoint, she said companies should "prioritise the health of their employees and if they need to communicate to customers that delivery will take a little longer, they should be willing to do that".

Amazon doesn't employ many of these workers directly she added, using subcontractors instead, potentially allowing it to sidestep questions over whether those workers should have been called to work on Friday evening.

The firm's founder, Jeff Bezos, has also been criticised after posting pictures of astronauts who had just returned from a space tourism trip aboard his Blue Origin rocket.

Later he tweeted: "The news from Edwardsville is tragic. We're heartbroken over the loss of our teammates there, and our thoughts and prayers are with their families and loved ones."

Amazon said it was donating $1m (£757,000) to the Edwardsville Community Foundation as well as providing relief supplies including transport, food and water.

37.title: 2021 Western Kentucky tornado
37.content:
2021 Western Kentucky tornado[![Image 1](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/7/70/2021_Mayfield%2C_Kentucky%2C_tornado.png/317px-2021_Mayfield%2C_Kentucky%2C_tornado.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2021_Mayfield,_Kentucky,_tornado.png)

[![Image 2: Weather radar showing intense precipitation over a geographical area](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Radar_of_the_Quad-State_Supercell_prior_to_impacting_Mayfield%2C_Kentucky.png/250px-Radar_of_the_Quad-State_Supercell_prior_to_impacting_Mayfield%2C_Kentucky.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radar_of_the_Quad-State_Supercell_prior_to_impacting_Mayfield,_Kentucky.png)

[![Image 3: Radar map shows strong tornado activity centered over parts of Arkansas, Missouri, and Tennessee, as well as predicted wind speeds for the storm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/SPC_Mesoscale_Discussion_1999.jpg/250px-SPC_Mesoscale_Discussion_1999.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SPC_Mesoscale_Discussion_1999.jpg)

[![Image 4: A collapsed slab of concrete with people looking at it on a grassy field](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/EF4_Damage_-_190_MPH_in_Bremen%2C_Kentucky.jpg/330px-EF4_Damage_-_190_MPH_in_Bremen%2C_Kentucky.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EF4_Damage_-_190_MPH_in_Bremen,_Kentucky.jpg)

*   **Clockwise from top:** The EF4 tornado illuminated by lightning near [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen,_Kentucky "Bremen, Kentucky") in [Muhlenberg County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhlenberg_County,_Kentucky "Muhlenberg County, Kentucky"); [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") mesoscale discussion of the tornado as it was ongoing; high-end EF4 damage to a home in [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen,_Kentucky "Bremen, Kentucky"); a [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEXRAD "NEXRAD") scan of the [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") showing the tornado as it struck Mayfield
Meteorological history
Formed December 10, 2021, 8:54 p.m. [CST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") ([UTC−06:00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC%E2%88%9206:00 "UTC−06:00"))
Dissipated December 10, 2021, 11:48 p.m. CST (UTC−06:00)
Duration 2 hours, 54 minutes[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-WKYTor-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2)
EF4 tornado
_on the [Enhanced Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced\_Fujita\_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")_
Max width 2,600 yd (1.5 mi; 2.4 km)
Path length 165.6 mi (266.5 km)
Highest winds 190 mph (310 km/h)
Overall effects
Fatalities 57 (+1 indirect)
Injuries 519
Areas affected[Obion County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obion_County,_Tennessee "Obion County, Tennessee") and Western Kentucky, United States
* * *

Part of the **[tornado outbreak of December 10–11, 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021 "Tornado outbreak of December 10–11, 2021") and [tornado outbreaks of 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_of_2021 "Tornadoes of 2021")**

During the late evening hours of Friday, December 10, 2021, a massive and devastating high-end [EF4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_Fujita_scale "Enhanced Fujita scale")[tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado"), sometimes referred to as the **Western Kentucky tornado**,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-3)**Mayfield tornado**,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-4) or **The Beast**,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-5) tracked a significant distance across Western Kentucky, United States, producing severe-to-catastrophic damage in numerous towns, including [Mayfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield,_Kentucky "Mayfield, Kentucky"), [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton,_Kentucky "Princeton, Kentucky"), [Dawson Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawson_Springs,_Kentucky "Dawson Springs, Kentucky"), and [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen,_Kentucky "Bremen, Kentucky").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2) This tornado was the second significant tornado in an exceedingly long-tracked tornado family; it began just inside northern [Obion County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obion_County,_Tennessee "Obion County, Tennessee")– a few miles after [another long-tracked tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tri-State_tornado "2021 Tri-State tornado") that traveled through northeast [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), the [Missouri Bootheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Bootheel "Missouri Bootheel"), and northwest [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee")– and dissipated in western Obion County.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-MEG-6) After crossing into [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky"), the tornado moved through eleven counties of the [Jackson Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Purchase "Jackson Purchase") and [Western Coal Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Coal_Field "Western Coal Field") regions, at times becoming wrapped in rain during its almost three-hour lifespan that covered 165.6 miles (266.5 km). It was the deadliest and longest-tracked tornado in [an outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021 "Tornado outbreak of December 10–11, 2021") that produced numerous, strong tornadoes in several states; this tornado caused 57 deaths.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2) The violent tornado became the first such [storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm "Storm") to impact Kentucky, ever since an [EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_2%E2%80%933,_2012#Crittenden%E2%80%93Piner%E2%80%93Morning_View,_Kentucky "Tornado outbreak of March 2–3, 2012") struck the state in 2012.

Early estimates suggested the tornado family, which some media outlets described as a "Quad-State tornado" due to the storm's long track and similarity to the 219-mile (352 km) [Tri-State tornado of 1925](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado"), might have traveled 250 miles (400 km) on the ground, making it the longest-tracked tornado in history.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Reynolds2-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:2-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:17-9) Storm surveys found the majority of the storm's path consisted of two separate EF4 tornadoes, and three weaker, short-lived tornadoes in between them in northwestern [Obion County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obion_County,_Tennessee "Obion County, Tennessee"). The parent [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that produced the two EF4 tornadoes, and eleven tornadoes in total, later became known as the Quad-State supercell.

After the tornado, a state of emergency and a federal disaster were declared by Governor [Andy Beshear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Beshear "Andy Beshear") and President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") on December 11. The death toll of 57 was the highest from a tornado in the month of December in U.S. history, while also being the deadliest tornado since [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_of_2011 "Tornadoes of 2011"). Some of the worst damage occurred in Mayfield and was considered by some [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") (NWS) analysts in a case study as bordering on EF5 intensity, prompting discussion on the intensity of high-end tornadoes and damage requirements.

Multiple workers at the [Mayfield Consumer Products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield_Consumer_Products "Mayfield Consumer Products") candle factory that was destroyed with multiple casualties alleged that supervisors told them they would be fired if they left their shifts early ahead of the storm's direct hit on the city. Company spokespeople have denied the allegations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:3-10) On December 17, it was reported that multiple workers (only one was named due to fear of [reprisal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reprisal "Reprisal")) filed a [class-action lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action "Class action") against the company. The lawsuit alleged that the company had up to three and a half hours to allow employees to leave before the tornado hit the factory and showed a flagrant indifference to the rights of the workers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-11)

Meteorological synopsis
-----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Meteorological synopsis")]

[![Image 5: Path of the tornadoes that struck Kentucky on December 10–11, 2021](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11%2C_2021.png/250px-Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11%2C_2021.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11,_2021.png)

Radar collage of a [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that spawned a [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family") during the outbreak

On December 8, 2021, the NWS [Storm Prediction Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center "Storm Prediction Center") (SPC) outlined a slight risk of severe weather across a broad area of the [Mississippi Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_Valley "Mississippi Valley"). Despite the potential for a higher-end severe threat to materialize, forecasters were uncertain about the extent of [instability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convective_available_potential_energy "Convective available potential energy"), degree of directional [wind shear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_shear "Wind shear"), and late timing[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] of potential storms.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_:18-12) The following day, the SPC noted an increased potential for organized severe thunderstorms in the region between southeastern Arkansas and southern [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana"), and upgraded that area to an enhanced risk[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_].[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_:19-13)

As an intense, upper-level [trough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trough_(meteorology) "Trough (meteorology)") progressed across the High Plains, with robust instability and moisture return across the Mississippi Valley, the SPC expanded the enhanced risk and introduced a moderate risk area from northeastern Arkansas into southern Illinois on the morning of December 10. Forecasters indicated atmospheric conditions favored the development of nocturnal supercells capable of producing long-tracked, strong tornadoes.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_:20-14)

At 3:00 p.m. [CST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone") (21:00[UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinated_Universal_Time "Coordinated Universal Time")), the SPC issued a [tornado watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_watch "Tornado watch") across the highest-risk area: central and eastern Arkansas, west Tennessee, northwestern Mississippi, southeastern Missouri, and southern portions of Illinois and Indiana; it was the first of eleven such warnings issued over the next few hours for the middle Mississippi Valley.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_:21-15) Initial storms developed across central Arkansas around 2:00 p.m. CST (20:00 UTC), and weaker activity developed over central Missouri around 90 minutes later. Additional clusters of thunderstorms developed over southwestern Missouri– forming between [Bolivar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivar,_Missouri "Bolivar, Missouri") and [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage,_Missouri "Carthage, Missouri"), eventually back-building into northeastern Oklahoma– and central Arkansas, forming southwest of [Hot Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Springs,_Arkansas "Hot Springs, Arkansas"), between 5:00 and 5:30 p.m. CST (23:00–23:30 UTC).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_:22-16) Though this activity lacked much vigor at its onset due to a strong capping inversion,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_:23-17) the convective cells began to show organization as they progressed eastward.

One storm that formed from the initial mid-afternoon activity near [Arkadelphia, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkadelphia,_Arkansas "Arkadelphia, Arkansas"), matured into a long-lived supercell as it progressed in an unstable, deeply moist, and highly sheared environment.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-18) This cell persisted for more than 550 miles (890 km) over several hours from eastern Arkansas to northeastern Kentucky, producing eleven tornadoes, two of which were large and intense. The cell started showing signs of surface-based rotation southwest of [Searcy, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Searcy,_Arkansas "Searcy, Arkansas"), around 5:30 p.m. CST (23:30 UTC). At 5:51 p.m. CST, the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service_North_Little_Rock,_Arkansas "National Weather Service North Little Rock, Arkansas") office in [North Little Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Little_Rock,_Arkansas "North Little Rock, Arkansas") issued the first tornado warning associated with the storm for portions of [Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Arkansas "Jackson County, Arkansas"), [Lawrence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_County,_Arkansas "Lawrence County, Arkansas"), [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_County,_Arkansas "White County, Arkansas"), and [Woodruff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodruff_County,_Arkansas "Woodruff County, Arkansas") counties.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-19) One of the first tornadoes associated with the storm, an EF0, touched down in western [Poinsett County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poinsett_County,_Arkansas "Poinsett County, Arkansas") near [Weiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weiner,_Arkansas "Weiner, Arkansas") around 6:40 p.m. CST; about fifteen minutes later, storm spotters reported a large tornado near [Greenfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenfield,_Arkansas "Greenfield, Arkansas"), prompting a [particularly dangerous situation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particularly_dangerous_situation "Particularly dangerous situation") (PDS) tornado warning for portions of [Poinsett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poinsett_County,_Arkansas "Poinsett County, Arkansas"), [Craighead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craighead_County,_Arkansas "Craighead County, Arkansas"), and [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_County,_Arkansas "Mississippi County, Arkansas") counties, including areas to the south of [Jonesboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonesboro,_Arkansas "Jonesboro, Arkansas").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-20)

[Doppler radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_radar "Weather radar") analysis estimated the supercell maintained a nearly continuous, high-end rotational vorticity signature, averaging 94 mph (151 km/h; 82 kn) for approximately four hours and twenty minutes, a rarity among thunderstorms that produce [mesocyclonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesocyclone "Mesocyclone") vorticity (averaging 1.5% of all supercells). The only velocities below the average recorded along the storm track were observed between 8:44 and 9:01 p.m. CST [02:44–3:01 UTC] as the storm crossed from Obion County, Tennessee, into [Hickman County, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickman_County,_Kentucky "Hickman County, Kentucky"). This time frame coincides with the start of the Western Kentucky tornado, implying the supercell underwent a mesocyclone re-strengthening phase during this period. During this intense tornado's lifetime, peak gate-to-gate velocities of 128 mph (206 km/h; 111 kn) were recorded at 9:58 p.m. CST (04:58 UTC) over northeastern [Marshall County, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_County,_Kentucky "Marshall County, Kentucky").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_wapo-1211-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_wapo-btn-23)

Elsewhere, multiple lines of intense storms, some with embedded supercells, developed across the Mississippi Valley region through the night, and generated other strong, long-lived tornadoes.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-25) By the pre-dawn hours of December 11, a decrease in instability led to a gradual weakening of a line of thunderstorms along the associated [cold front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_front "Cold front") from eastern Kentucky southward into central Alabama.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-27)

The SPC issued a record-setting 43 [mesoscale discussions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_Prediction_Center#Mesoscale_discussions "Storm Prediction Center") (MCDs) between 12:00 p.m. UTC December 10 and 12:00 p.m. UTC December 11, all of which were associated with the broader storm system. Thirty-eight of these were convective discussions relating to severe thunderstorm activity, and five were non-convective discussions relating to heavy snow associated with the system that concurrently fell across much of the [Upper Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Midwest "Upper Midwest").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-28) Through the night, the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") (NWS) issued 149 tornado warnings across Arkansas, Tennessee, Missouri, Mississippi, Kentucky, Illinois, and Indiana.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-29)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021_wapo-btn-23) These included multiple PDS tornado warnings and [tornado emergencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_emergency "Tornado emergency") in Arkansas, Tennessee, Kentucky, and Missouri. Eight of the tornado warnings issued by the NWS offices in [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee "Memphis, Tennessee"), and [Paducah, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paducah,_Kentucky "Paducah, Kentucky"), during the event were tornado emergencies, the most ever issued during the month of December, breaking the previous record of three issued on [December 23, 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_December_23%E2%80%9325,_2015 "Tornado outbreak of December 23–25, 2015").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-31)
