English [Wikisource](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikisource "Wikisource") has original text related to this article:

### Formation and rapid strengthening

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Formation and rapid strengthening")]

The tornado touched down in [Woodland Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland_Mills,_Tennessee "Woodland Mills, Tennessee") in [Obion County, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obion_County,_Tennessee "Obion County, Tennessee"), along Woodland Mills Road at 8:54 p.m. CST (02:54 UTC). It was produced by the same supercell that had produced another [violent long-tracked tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tri-State_tornado "2021 Tri-State tornado") that affected northeast [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), the [Missouri Bootheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri_Bootheel "Missouri Bootheel"), and northwest [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"). After the dissipation of that tornado in Obion County northeast of [Samburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samburg,_Tennessee "Samburg, Tennessee"), the supercell produced three weak, brief tornadoes before the Western Kentucky tornado formed several miles to the northeast.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32) The tornado initially moved through the north side of Woodland Mills, causing minor damage to roofs and trees, before crossing [SR 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_State_Route_5 "Tennessee State Route 5"). After moving northeast for one-half mile (0.80 km), rated EF0, it crossed the Tennessee–Kentucky state line near the community of [State Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Line,_Kentucky "State Line, Kentucky") in [Fulton County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulton_County,_Kentucky "Fulton County, Kentucky"), causing additional tree damage. The total damage caused in Tennessee by the tornado was estimated at $25,000 (2021 USD).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-33)

[![Image 7: The tornado destroyed everything in sight, leaving only debris and the foundations of buildings](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/EF4_damage_to_a_business_in_Cayce.jpg/250px-EF4_damage_to_a_business_in_Cayce.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:EF4_damage_to_a_business_in_Cayce.jpg)

Low-end EF4 damage to a business in downtown Cayce

Farther to the northeast, the tornado reached EF2 strength, tearing roofs off homes, damaging or destroying outbuildings, damaging irrigation equipment, and ripping apart trailer homes. Soon after, the tornado became violent and directly impacted the small community of [Cayce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayce,_Kentucky "Cayce, Kentucky") at low-end EF4 intensity, where homes and small businesses were damaged or destroyed, some of which were leveled or swept from their foundations. A music venue in a former school building was badly damaged, and the Cayce Volunteer Fire Department building was destroyed; the metal beams of the structure severely twisted as pieces of heavy machinery were tossed around. Several outbuildings and mobile homes were also destroyed. One person died in Cayce and several others were injured.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

After moving to the northeast of Cayce, the tornado weakened but remained strong as it moved at EF3 intensity through rural areas to the northeast of the town, destroying barns and a cell tower, and tearing the roof and exterior walls from a house. The tornado moved into [Hickman County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickman_County,_Kentucky "Hickman County, Kentucky") and appeared to dramatically intensify as it crossed [US 51](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_51_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 51 in Kentucky"), where extreme ground scouring occurred in nearby fields. The tornado scoured trenches into the ground, removing all grass and several inches of topsoil in the worst affected areas.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-34) No structures were impacted near US 51 and no rating was applied to the scouring. EF3 damage continued past this point as homes and metal truss towers were destroyed. EF2 damage was noted as it tracked into [Graves County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graves_County,_Kentucky "Graves County, Kentucky"), closely paralleling [Purchase Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purchase_Parkway "Purchase Parkway") and [US 45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_45_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 45 in Kentucky"), and moving directly toward the city of [Mayfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield,_Kentucky "Mayfield, Kentucky"). The roof of a house along [KY 339](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_339 "Kentucky Route 339") was torn off, and many trees and power poles were downed in this area.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-auto-35)

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Urban_Search_and_Rescue_Team_IN-TF1_DOD_108727472.webm "Play video")[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Urban_Search_and_Rescue_Team_IN-TF1_DOD_108727472.webm)

Search and rescue teams combing through the wreckage of the Mayfield Consumer Products candle factory in Mayfield on December 13

The National Weather Service issued a tornado emergency for Mayfield at 9:26 p.m. CST (03:26 UTC) as the now massive wedge tornado approached the town from the southwest.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-auto-35) As the tornado entered Mayfield, it regained EF4 intensity, and numerous homes along Cardinal Road were damaged or destroyed; some houses were leveled or swept from their foundations. Trees in the area were debarked and denuded, cars were thrown, and mobile homes were destroyed. EF4 damage continued after the tornado crossed over [Mayfield Bypass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_45_in_Kentucky#Mayfield_bypass "U.S. Route 45 in Kentucky") (US 45 Bypass/[I-69](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_69_in_Kentucky "Interstate 69 in Kentucky")), where [Mayfield Consumer Products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield_Consumer_Products "Mayfield Consumer Products"), a candle factory where approximately 110 employees were working, was flattened.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-nbcnews2-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Brinkmann-37) The large, metal-framed warehouse building collapsed, trapping employees, and resulting in eight deaths and numerous injuries.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-D'Angelo-39)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-nbcnews2-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Brinkmann-37) Allegedly, workers' jobs had been threatened by supervisors if they left the factory between the first and second tornado warnings for the area– a tornado warning had been issued at approximately 5:30 p.m. CST that evening– and again after the second tornado warning was issued after 9:00 p.m. CST.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:3-10) Several nearby industrial businesses were also damaged or destroyed, while semi-trucks and other industrial vehicles were thrown and destroyed, some being left unrecognizable.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_National_Bank_Mayfield_CCTV.webm "Play video")[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_National_Bank_Mayfield_CCTV.webm)

CCTV footage of the tornado striking a bank in downtown Mayfield at EF4 intensity

After briefly weakening to EF3 intensity, the tornado again intensified, reaching just below high-end EF4 intensity as it moved along [US 45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_45_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 45 in Kentucky") and tore through the center of Mayfield, resulting in widespread, catastrophic damage throughout the [historic downtown square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayfield_Downtown_Commercial_District "Mayfield Downtown Commercial District") that was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Register_of_Historic_Places "National Register of Historic Places") for its [late-Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_architecture "Victorian architecture") and [Classical Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") architecture.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-courier-journal-41) Most of the structures in downtown Mayfield were heavily damaged or destroyed, including large, well-built, multi-story, brick buildings that collapsed. Only large piles of bricks and lumber remained in the hardest-hit portions of the downtown area, and streets were left buried under debris. The large, well-constructed [Graves County Courthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graves_County_Courthouse "Graves County Courthouse") had much of its roof torn off, its [clock tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clock_tower "Clock tower") collapsed, and some of its exterior upper-floor walls were demolished.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-42) Several restaurants, an indoor soccer facility, a barber shop, automotive business, a gym, a bank, a movie theater, a health-and-rehab center, and many other businesses in downtown Mayfield were destroyed. Large metal silos were crumpled and heavily damaged at a granary, and the large Mayfield water tower was toppled and destroyed. The post office, city hall, fire station, and police station were significantly damaged or destroyed, and the emergency operations center lost the ability to transmit radio communications.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-nbcnews2-36)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

Three large churches were destroyed in downtown Mayfield, including the First Presbyterian Church: a large, well-built brick structure that was mostly leveled. The domed roof and upper walls of the First Christian Church collapsed, as did the sanctuary of the First United Methodist Church, which was constructed with very thick, masonry, exterior walls. A school bus garage, metal industrial buildings, and apartment buildings in other parts of the town were damaged or destroyed. The tornado also devastated residential areas of the town, levelling or sweeping numerous homes from their foundations. Many trees were denuded and debarked, and cars were thrown hundreds of yards and mangled. [Dual polarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_radar#Polarization "Weather radar") radar imagery showed the tornado had lofted debris up to 30,000 feet (9,100 m) as it impacted the city.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-43) Twenty-two people were killed in and around Mayfield, and hundreds more were injured, many severely.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-lexhl-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-46) The tornado's winds peaked at 188 mph (303 km/h) in the city.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

### Marshall, Lyon, and Caldwell counties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Marshall, Lyon, and Caldwell counties")]

After leaving Mayfield, the tornado weakened, producing damage at EF2 to EF3 strength, and continued northeast along [I-69](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_69_in_Kentucky "Interstate 69 in Kentucky") and [KY 58](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_58 "Kentucky Route 58"). A hangar and some small airplanes were destroyed at Mayfield Graves County Airport, and homes, a nearby church, and a business were damaged. Further weakening occurred as the tornado continued moving northeast, and EF0 to EF1 damage to trees and structures occurred. It intensified again as it approached and crossed the [Marshall County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_County,_Kentucky "Marshall County, Kentucky") line along I-69 before moving through the northwestern and northern outskirts of [Benton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benton,_Kentucky "Benton, Kentucky"), damaging or destroying homes, garages, and outbuildings; downing trees and power lines; and flipping RV campers. Most of the damage through this section of Marshall County ranged in intensity from EF2 to EF3, though a few homes to the southwest of Benton were leveled or swept from their foundations at high-end EF3 strength.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-47) The tornado then moved into [Briensburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Briensburg,_Kentucky "Briensburg, Kentucky") at EF2 intensity; houses near and along [US 68](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_68 "U.S. Route 68") sustained partial-to-total roof loss, outbuildings were damaged or destroyed, and a metal truss transmission tower collapsed. Past Briensburg, EF3 damage occurred along Lowery Road, where a poorly anchored house was leveled, and some other homes sustained EF2 damage.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

[![Image 8: Aerial view of destroyed homes and trees after a hurricane](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Aerial_imagery_of_widespread_destruction_in_Cambridge_Shores%2C_where_the_tornado_impacted_at_low-end_EF4_intensity.jpg/250px-Aerial_imagery_of_widespread_destruction_in_Cambridge_Shores%2C_where_the_tornado_impacted_at_low-end_EF4_intensity.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aerial_imagery_of_widespread_destruction_in_Cambridge_Shores,_where_the_tornado_impacted_at_low-end_EF4_intensity.jpg)

Aerial imagery of widespread destruction in Cambridge Shores, where the tornado impacted at low-end EF4 intensity

The tornado again reached EF4 intensity as it moved through the small community of Cambridge Shores, on the western shore of [Kentucky Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Lake "Kentucky Lake"). Numerous homes, including large lakeside houses, were leveled or swept from their foundations. Large trees were snapped, denuded, and debarked, and vehicles were thrown. The roof of a fire department building was torn off and large, metal, boat-storage buildings were destroyed. The tornado then weakened but remained strong as it crossed Kentucky Lake into [Lyon County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyon_County,_Kentucky "Lyon County, Kentucky") and traversed the [Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Between_the_Lakes_National_Recreation_Area "Land Between the Lakes National Recreation Area"), leveling a large swath of trees and snapping power poles at EF2 strength as it passed near [Twin Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Lakes,_Kentucky "Twin Lakes, Kentucky") before crossing [Lake Barkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Barkley "Lake Barkley"). After crossing Lake Barkley, the tornado strengthened back to EF3 intensity, and crossed [KY 93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_93 "Kentucky Route 93") and [I-24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_24 "Interstate 24") near the lake's eastern shore, where many homes sustained major damage or were destroyed, and several houses were leveled or swept from their foundations.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

Soon after, the tornado again explosively intensified and crossed into [Caldwell County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caldwell_County,_Kentucky "Caldwell County, Kentucky") along [KY 293](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_293 "Kentucky Route 293"), producing EF4 damage as it impacted the southern edge of [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton,_Kentucky "Princeton, Kentucky"), where another tornado emergency was issued.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-48) Two miles (3.2 km) before impacting Princeton, the tornado hit and destroyed a Kentucky [mesonet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesonet "Mesonet") station, which recorded 120.1 miles per hour (193.3 km/h) winds, setting the new record for the highest-measured wind gust in Kentucky history.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-NCEI_Wind-49) Within two-miles, the tornado intensified to a minimum of 60 miles per hour (97 km/h).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-NCEI_Wind-49) In Princeton, dozens of houses along the southern and southeastern fringes of town were destroyed, especially at the Princeton Golf and Country Club subdivision, where several houses were leveled or swept away. The [University of Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Kentucky "University of Kentucky") Research Center was destroyed; metal roof trusses were carried hundreds of yards from the structure and wrapped around trees. Cars were thrown from the parking lot into adjacent fields, metal light poles were ripped from their concrete footings, and ground scouring occurred.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-50)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS "Wikipedia:NOTRS")_] In and around Princeton, trees were stripped of their limbs and partially debarked, barns and farm buildings were destroyed, livestock was killed, and cycloidal markings were left in fields outside the town. Four deaths and numerous injuries occurred in Princeton. The tornado then followed [US 62](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_62_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 62 in Kentucky"), producing EF2 to EF3 damage to homes in the small communities of [Lewistown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewistown,_Kentucky "Lewistown, Kentucky") and [Midway](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Midway,_Caldwell_County,_Kentucky&action=edit&redlink=1 "Midway, Caldwell County, Kentucky (page does not exist)").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

### Dawson Springs, Barnsley, and Bremen

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Dawson Springs, Barnsley, and Bremen")]

[![Image 9: Remains of the destroyed town with rubble and destroyed buildings on the ground](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Dawson_springs_EF4_%282%29.jpg/250px-Dawson_springs_EF4_%282%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dawson_springs_EF4_(2).jpg)

Widespread destruction in a residential area of Dawson Springs

Past Midway, the tornado became violent and again reached EF4 intensity as it moved along [US 62](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_62_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 62 in Kentucky"), causing catastrophic damage as it entered the city of [Dawson Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawson_Springs,_Kentucky "Dawson Springs, Kentucky"), located along the Caldwell–[Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins_County,_Kentucky "Hopkins County, Kentucky") county line. A fourth tornado emergency was in effect for Dawson Springs and [St. Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Charles,_Kentucky "St. Charles, Kentucky") as the storm moved through the area. In residential areas in northern Dawson Springs, entire blocks of homes were destroyed, and many houses were leveled or swept from their foundations. Cars were thrown, copious amounts of structural debris were strewn in all directions, countless trees were shredded and debarked, and only rubble remained in the hardest-hit neighborhoods. The Dawson Village apartment complex was destroyed and several two-story, brick apartment buildings sustained EF4 damage, being largely reduced to rubble with only a few first-floor interior walls left intact. The apartment complex had structural flaws and estimated failure wind speeds of 155 miles per hour (249 km/h).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:1-51) Vehicles were thrown into piles in the parking lot of the complex. Several [duplexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duplex_(building) "Duplex (building)") at Clarkdale Court were destroyed, including one that was leveled with only a pile of debris remaining. An [American Legion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Legion "American Legion") post and a car wash were flattened, and a church and a medical clinic sustained major damage. Some logistics facilities and warehouses in an industrial park were leveled as the tornado exited the city, as were several metal self-storage-unit buildings and large garages nearby.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-52)

Fourteen people were killed in the Dawson Springs area and many others were injured. A mother and her two children survived with major injuries by hanging on to a mattress as they were thrown 250 feet (76 m) through the air into a field after the tornado swept their Dawson Springs home from its foundation after crushing them underneath it first.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-courier-journal-41)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-53) A photograph from a destroyed house in Dawson Springs was lofted and transported almost 130 miles (210 km) by the intense tornadic updrafts, eventually being found in [New Albany, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Albany,_Indiana "New Albany, Indiana").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-54)

[![Image 10: Derailment of freight train car with broken axles, debris, and a bare tree in the background](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/BarnsleyFreightCar2021.jpg/250px-BarnsleyFreightCar2021.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BarnsleyFreightCar2021.jpg)

A multi-ton railroad freight car that was thrown from the tracks in Barnsley

Beyond Dawson Springs, the tornado tracked to the northeast, passing north of [Ilsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilsley,_Kentucky "Ilsley, Kentucky") and through the rural community of Carbondale, weakening slightly to high-end EF3 strength but continuing to cause major damage. Farm outbuildings and mobile homes were demolished, and houses sustained major damage or were destroyed. Additional high-end EF3 damage occurred and another tornado emergency was issued as it moved through [Barnsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnsley,_Kentucky "Barnsley, Kentucky"), just south of [Earlington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earlington,_Kentucky "Earlington, Kentucky") and [Helca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecla,_Kentucky "Hecla, Kentucky"), and just north of [Mortons Gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortons_Gap,_Kentucky "Mortons Gap, Kentucky").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-55) Almost every house in the small community was damaged or destroyed, including some that were leveled, though they were not well-constructed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32) A train on the [CSX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation")[Henderson Subdivision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henderson_Subdivision "Henderson Subdivision") adjacent to [US 41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_41_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 41 in Kentucky") in the town was derailed, as were 25 multi-ton freight cars, several of which were thrown from the tracks; one was tossed into a house.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Courier1-56) Thousands of large trees were downed and vehicles were flipped. Past Barnsley, the tornado crossed over the CSX Cut-Off Main line and [I-69](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_69_in_Kentucky "Interstate 69 in Kentucky") before passing through an unpopulated, swampy area, where large trees were snapped or uprooted, and damage was rated EF2.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

Continuing into northern [Muhlenberg County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhlenberg_County,_Kentucky "Muhlenberg County, Kentucky"), another tornado emergency was issued for the community of [Bremen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bremen,_Kentucky "Bremen, Kentucky") as the tornado approached from the southwest. It abruptly intensified to its peak intensity of high-end EF4 strength with estimated winds of 190 mph (310 km/h) winds as it crossed and paralleled [KY 175](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kentucky_supplemental_roads_and_rural_secondary_highways_(1%E2%80%93199)#KY_175 "List of Kentucky supplemental roads and rural secondary highways (1–199)") through the north side of town. Many homes were destroyed along this portion of its path, including several that were completely swept away with little debris remaining. Large trees were denuded and debarked, grass was scoured from the ground, and vehicles were thrown through the air and mangled. Some of the worst damage in Bremen occurred along Bethlehem Cemetery Road, where a row of four homes were completely swept away with only their foundations remaining, and debris was scattered long distances through fields across the street. Concrete floor slabs were torn from the foundation of one home and shattered, while the paved driveway of another residence was cracked and scoured. Houses that were farther away from the center of the damage path sustained roof and exterior wall loss. Mobile homes, barns, garages, and other outbuildings were also destroyed. At Bethlehem Baptist Church, a brick exterior wall was blown out and was shifted slightly off of its foundation, while Church Street General Baptist Church lost much of its roof.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-58)

Eleven people were killed in and around Bremen, and others were injured.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-59) Among the fatalities was District Judge Brian Crick, who represented Muhlenberg and [McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLean_County,_Kentucky "McLean County, Kentucky") counties, as confirmed in a statement from the Supreme Court of Kentucky on December 11.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-60) After the tornado left Bremen, some weakening occurred; it crossed [US 431](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_431_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 431 in Kentucky") south of Stroud, where some houses and mobile homes were damaged or destroyed, and hundreds of large trees were snapped and denuded. Damage in this area was rated EF2 to low-end EF3.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

### Later damage and dissipation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Later damage and dissipation")]

[![Image 11: The house and surrounding area has been destroyed by a tornado](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Hartford_KY_tornado_damage.jpg/250px-Hartford_KY_tornado_damage.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hartford_KY_tornado_damage.jpg)

Major structural damage to a house near Hartford

While passing near the Muhlenberg–[McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLean_County,_Kentucky "McLean County, Kentucky") county line, the tornado weakened substantially as it crossed into [Ohio County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_County,_Kentucky "Ohio County, Kentucky") at 11:10 p.m. (05:10 UTC), producing EF1 damage as it traversed rugged, hilly terrain to the west of [Centertown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centertown,_Kentucky "Centertown, Kentucky").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32) It moved through an abandoned coal-strip mine, overturning a large section of a coal conveyor belt, snapping trees, and downing power poles. A few farm outbuildings in this area were also damaged or destroyed. The tornado again strengthened north of Centertown along [KY 85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_85 "Kentucky Route 85"), producing EF2 damage; houses and outbuildings were damaged or destroyed, including a well-built house where much of the roof was torn off and an exterior wall collapsed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32) Five large chicken houses were destroyed, and hundreds of large, hardwood trees along a one-quarter-mile (400 m)-wide swath along this section of the path were snapped and uprooted. Weakening back to EF1 intensity, the tornado downed trees along Carter Ferry Road and Mud College Road.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

The tornado entered a flatter area to the west of [Hartford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Kentucky "Hartford, Kentucky") and began to intensify once more; large steel power poles were bent over or broken along Johnson School Road, earning an EF3 rating. North of Hartford, the tornado crossed [US 231](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_231_in_Kentucky "U.S. Route 231 in Kentucky"), [I-165](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_165_(Kentucky) "Interstate 165 (Kentucky)"), and [KY 69](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_69 "Kentucky Route 69"), and crossed the [Rough River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_River "Rough River") three times.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2) Homes and businesses sustained significant EF3 damage in this area; two tractor-trailers were lifted and thrown 40 yards (37 m), and one of the cabs was mangled. Houses, barns, garages, a small brick office structure, silos, and a fertilizer storage facility were destroyed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-LMKOhio-61) The last area of EF3-strength damage occurred along KY 69 and Utley Drive northeast of Hartford, where a poorly anchored, block-foundation home was swept away and destroyed, and other houses lost their roofs and exterior walls. Two anchored mobile homes were swept away and destroyed, with their frames tossed and bent, and one was thrown 100 yards (91 m). An RV camper in this area was thrown 30 yards (27 m), landing upside down; tractors and hay bales were also thrown considerable distances.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-LMKOhio-61) Damage of up to EF2 intensity occurred beyond this point as the tornado crossed Humble Valley Road, Halls Creek Road, and Mount Vernon Road before passing north of [Olaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olaton,_Kentucky "Olaton, Kentucky"). Homes were significantly damaged, barns and mobile homes were destroyed, a cow was killed, and thousands of large hardwood trees were downed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32) The tornado paralleled the Ohio–Grayson county line and very briefly crossed a bend in the Rough River into [Grayson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grayson_County,_Kentucky "Grayson County, Kentucky"). Hundreds of trees along Cane Ford Road were downed and an abandoned trailer home was destroyed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

The tornado then crossed [KY 54](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_54 "Kentucky Route 54"), where the last area of EF2 damage occurred, as a frail home was destroyed and left with only a few walls standing. Large trees were snapped and one of them fell on and destroyed a car. Some outbuildings in this area were also damaged or destroyed. Entering [Breckinridge County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breckinridge_County,_Kentucky "Breckinridge County, Kentucky") at EF1 intensity, the tornado paralleled the Breckinridge–Grayson county line and crossed [KY 110](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Kentucky_supplemental_roads_and_rural_secondary_highways_(1%E2%80%93199)#KY_110 "List of Kentucky supplemental roads and rural secondary highways (1–199)") northwest of [Falls of Rough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falls_of_Rough,_Kentucky "Falls of Rough, Kentucky"). Hundreds of trees in the area were downed and two structures sustained minor damage. The tornado downed power lines as it crossed [KY 79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Route_79 "Kentucky Route 79") at EF0 strength, damaged a large boat-storage facility, and scattered sheet metal debris across the runway of a small airport. Some additional minor tree damage occurred before the tornado dissipated near Park Drive in Grayson County at 11:48 p.m. CST (5:48 UTC) as it entered [Rough River Dam State Resort Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_River_Dam_State_Resort_Park "Rough River Dam State Resort Park") near Rough River Lake, approximately four miles (6.4 km) west of [McDaniels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDaniels,_Kentucky "McDaniels, Kentucky").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)

### Possible EF5 intensity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Possible EF5 intensity")]

[![Image 12: Purple vertical cloud extending over a multicolored ground, with the label Mayfield visible on the ground](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Tornadic_Debris_lofted_over_30%2C000_feet.jpg/250px-Tornadic_Debris_lofted_over_30%2C000_feet.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tornadic_Debris_lofted_over_30,000_feet.jpg)

Radar 3D volume scan of the supercell showing debris lofted over 30,000 feet (9.1 km) in the air as the tornado struck Mayfield

In 2022, [Timothy Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_P._Marshall "Timothy P. Marshall"), a meteorologist, [structural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_engineer "Structural engineer") and [forensic engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forensic_engineering "Forensic engineering"); Zachary B. Wienhoff, with Haag Engineering Company; Christine L. Wielgos, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service of Paducah; and Brian E. Smith, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service of Omaha, published a damage survey of portions of the tornado's track, particularly through Mayfield and Dawson Springs. The report notes: "the tornado damage rating might have been higher had more wind resistant structures been encountered. Also, the fast forward speed of the tornado had little 'dwell' time of strong winds over a building and thus, the damage likely would have been more severe if the tornado were slower."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:1-51) Marshall later stated in 2023 that the Western Kentucky tornado was "the closest to EF5 that I can remember" since the [Moore EF5 of 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Moore_tornado "2013 Moore tornado"). Marshall also stated some of the buildings struck by the strongest winds "were horribly constructed and could not resist 100 or even 150 mph wind let alone 200 mph", meaning it was "impossible to know if EF5 winds affected them".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-WashPost-62)

On January 23, 2025, Anthony W. Lyza with the [National Severe Storms Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Severe_Storms_Laboratory "National Severe Storms Laboratory") along with Harold E. Brooks and Makenzie J. Kroca with the [University of Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oklahoma "University of Oklahoma") published a paper where they stated the tornado in Mayfield was an "EF5 candidate" and opined that the EF5 starting wind speed should be 190 mph (306 km/h) instead of 201 mph (323 km/h).[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-63)

[![Image 13: Aerial shot of a residential area heavily damaged by a tornado, with debris scattered across the landscape](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Mayfield_KY_State_Farm_CRU_-23.jpg/250px-Mayfield_KY_State_Farm_CRU_-23.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mayfield_KY_State_Farm_CRU_-23.jpg)

Aerial view of EF3 damage in Mayfield the day after the tornado

The tornado reached a peak width of 2,600 yards (2,400 m) and was on the ground for nearly three hours, tracking 165.6 miles (266.5 km) from Woodland Mills to Rough River Dam State Resort Park.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-DAT-32)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-LMKOhio-61)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:1-51) The path was the ninth longest in recorded history.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-SPCReview-64) It was rated high-end EF4 with an estimated peak wind speed of 190 mph (310 km/h).

The tornado directly killed 57 people and resulted in 519 injuries; it was the deadliest tornado ever recorded in the United States in the month of December, and the deadliest tornado since the [Joplin, Missouri tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado") on May 22, 2011.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2) In Graves County, 24 people died and more than 200 were injured; fifteen died in Hopkins County, eleven in Muhlenberg County, four in Caldwell County, and one person each in Fulton, Marshall, and Lyon counties.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2) A 58th victim suffered a heart attack while clearing debris and is listed as an indirect fatality.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-WKYTor-1)

The tornado produced profound destruction in multiple communities. In Mayfield, more than 4,000 structures were damaged or destroyed, including 3,778 residences, 183 commercial buildings, and 103 other structures.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-PAH-2) The tornado destroyed primarily low-income rental housing units, leading to a depleted stock of affordable housing in the city; Mayfield Housing Authority reported it had more than 700 requests for one-bedroom units almost a year after the tornado.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-65)

In Marshall County, containing the heavily damaged community of Cambridge Shores, 356 structures were destroyed or made uninhabitable, and 341 more sustained light or moderate damage.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-WKYTor-1) In Muhlenberg County, the tornado caused an estimated $7 million in agricultural damage alone, according to the University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension Office.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-66)

Response and recovery
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Response and recovery")]

[![Image 14: Damage caused by tornado in Mayfield, Kentucky](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/DawsonSpringsDamageIMG_0285.jpg/250px-DawsonSpringsDamageIMG_0285.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DawsonSpringsDamageIMG_0285.jpg)

Debris and destroyed homes along Alexander Street in Dawson Springs

On December 11, 2021, Kentucky governor [Andy Beshear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Beshear "Andy Beshear") declared a [state of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") for parts of western Kentucky; it was followed that day by U.S. president [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")'s approval of a federal emergency [disaster declaration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disaster_area "Disaster area") for the state of Kentucky.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-Hatter-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-apnews-68) Beshear also announced the creation of a tornado relief fund and asked people to donate blood.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-apnews-68) On December 15, Mayor of Mayfield Kathy Stewart O'Nan said that recovery efforts would continue.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-69) The NWS office in [Paducah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paducah,_Kentucky "Paducah, Kentucky") requested mental-health officers be present to assist meteorologists for potential trauma from assessing the tornado's path of devastation.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-70)

On December 12, [Federal Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Emergency_Management_Agency "Federal Emergency Management Agency") (FEMA) Administrator [Deanne Criswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deanne_Criswell "Deanne Criswell") and [U.S. Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security "United States Department of Homeland Security") Secretary [Alejandro Mayorkas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Mayorkas "Alejandro Mayorkas") visited areas of Graves and Marshall counties, met with emergency management officials and responders, and held a media briefing with Governor Beshear.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-71) Their visit was followed on December 15 by a visit from President Biden, who flew to Kentucky and toured Mayfield and Dawson Springs, meeting survivors. Describing the damage as "almost beyond belief", Biden announced that the disaster declaration had been amended to have the federal government pay the entire cost of debris removal, and overtime for law enforcement and emergency personnel for the next month.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-72)

The tornado's major impacts on Graves County Court operations, which included the destruction of the courthouse in Mayfield, led the [Kentucky Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Supreme_Court "Kentucky Supreme Court") to suspend the county's court operations, including physical and electronic court filings, between December 13, 2021, and January 11, 2022.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-73)

The _Mayfield Messenger_, the city's main newspaper, began printing an extra 2,000 copies per printing run of its paper, distributing them for free around the city.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-74)

By February 14, 2022, the [U.S. Army Corps of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Corps_of_Engineers "U.S. Army Corps of Engineers") had cleared more than 280,000 cubic yards (210,000 m 3) of debris in Graves County, including Mayfield;[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-75) by April 4, that number had risen to 265,453 cubic yards (202,953 m 3) of debris removed in Mayfield and 433,408 cubic yards (331,364 m 3) in total form Graves County.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-76) By May 2022, the [Tennessee Valley Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Valley_Authority "Tennessee Valley Authority") and the environmental nonprofit Living Lands and Waters, using excavators, barges, and volunteers, had removed 1.2 million pounds (540 metric tons) of tornado debris from [Kentucky Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky_Lake "Kentucky Lake"). Objects found included entire docks, cars, kayaks, and personal effects.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-79)

Governor Beshear's administration created the Team Western Kentucky Tornado Relief Fund, which received approximately 150,000 individual donations for a total of $52 million.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-80) Disaster-relief and humanitarian groups such as the [American Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Red_Cross "American Red Cross"), [The Salvation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Salvation_Army "The Salvation Army"), and [World Vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Vision_United_States "World Vision United States") collected donations and provided aid.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-apnews-68) More than 4,500 people attended a tornado relief concert in August 2022.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-81)

In 2024, the City of Mayfield was awarded $31.5 million in federal-and-state grants to help rebuild roads in its downtown area. The U.S. Department of Transportation awarded the city $25 million through its [Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebuilding_American_Infrastructure_with_Sustainability_and_Equity "Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity") (RAISE) grant program. That money, along with $6.3 million in state transportation funding and $200,000 from other federal grants, was to be used to reconstruct around 2.5 miles (4.0 km) of high-traffic thoroughfares in the Graves County seat.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-82)

In June 2022, Mayfield City Council put several blocks in the city's heavily impacted downtown under a building permit freeze as they decided how to rebuild in the area, before [rezoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoning "Zoning") the area in December 2022 for "less restrictive" commercial and residential [mixed-use development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-use_development "Mixed-use development").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-83) In December 2022, a temporary memorial was placed in the Mayfield court square.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-84) In February 2023, Mayfield mayor Kathy O'Nan visited [Louisville, Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisville,_Mississippi "Louisville, Mississippi"), which was struck by [a devastating EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Louisville,_Mississippi_tornado "2014 Louisville, Mississippi tornado") in 2014, to tour the damage path and speak with city leaders about the rebuilding process and funding sources.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-85)

### Mayfield candle factory lawsuit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Mayfield candle factory lawsuit")]

The Mayfield Consumer Products candle factory building collapsed, causing eight deaths and numerous injuries.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-D'Angelo-39) Accusations of factory management prohibiting workers from leaving before the tornado struck the factory were reported on December 13.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-:3-10)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-86) Workers said management told them: "if you leave, you're more than likely to be fired".[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-87) On December 17, it was reported multiple workers at the candle factory filed a lawsuit against Mayfield Consumer Products in state court, seeking compensation and punitive damages. The lawsuit alleged the factory had up to three-and-a-half hours to let workers leave as safety precautions and did not, and the company showed a "flagrant indifference to the rights of workers" and violated the Kentucky occupational safety and health workplace standards by refusing evacuations.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-88) The following January, the factory closed and Mayfield Consumer Products laid off approximately 250 workers there, shifting operations and the remaining workers to a new plant in the nearby town of [Hickory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickory,_Kentucky "Hickory, Kentucky").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-89)

On December 8, 2022, a second lawsuit was filed against Mayfield Consumer Products on behalf of three workers who were killed in the candle factory collapse and seven who survived. The lawsuit alleged "false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and violation of Kentucky statutory law".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado#cite_note-90)

After deadly Edwardsville tornado, Illinois lawmakers pass warehouse safety bill
================================================================================

St. Louis Public Radio | By [Will Bauer](https://www.stlpr.org/people/will-bauer)

Published June 6, 2025 at 5:00 AM CDT

*   [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=212153886819126&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.stlpr.org%2Fgovernment-politics-issues%2F2025-06-06%2Fafter-deadly-edwardsville-tornado-illinois-lawmakers-pass-warehouse-safety-bill)
*   [Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.stlpr.org%2Fgovernment-politics-issues%2F2025-06-06%2Fafter-deadly-edwardsville-tornado-illinois-lawmakers-pass-warehouse-safety-bill&text=After%20deadly%20Edwardsville%20tornado%2C%20Illinois%20lawmakers%20pass%20warehouse%20safety%20bill)
*   [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.stlpr.org%2Fgovernment-politics-issues%2F2025-06-06%2Fafter-deadly-edwardsville-tornado-illinois-lawmakers-pass-warehouse-safety-bill&mini=true&title=After%20deadly%20Edwardsville%20tornado%2C%20Illinois%20lawmakers%20pass%20warehouse%20safety%20bill&summary=The%20Illinois%20General%20Assembly%20passed%20the%20Warehouse%20Tornado%20Preparedness%20Act%20%E2%80%94%20a%20bill%20that%20addresses%20issues%20from%20the%20fatal%20Edwardsville%20tornado%20in%202021.&source=STLPR)
*   [Email](mailto:?body=After%20deadly%20Edwardsville%20tornado%2C%20Illinois%20lawmakers%20pass%20warehouse%20safety%20bill%0A%0Ahttps%3A%2F%2Fwww.stlpr.org%2Fgovernment-politics-issues%2F2025-06-06%2Fafter-deadly-edwardsville-tornado-illinois-lawmakers-pass-warehouse-safety-bill%0A%0AThe%20Illinois%20General%20Assembly%20passed%20the%20Warehouse%20Tornado%20Preparedness%20Act%20%E2%80%94%20a%20bill%20that%20addresses%20issues%20from%20the%20fatal%20Edwardsville%20tornado%20in%202021.)

    ![Image 4: An EF-3 tornado on December 10, 2021 flattened half of an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville — killing six people.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c5b2662/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x2112+0+0/resize/880x620!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fe3%2F8a%2F55a0c85b4d2da5f307c85e197c72%2F12112021-bm-amazon-storms-003.jpg)

Brian Munoz

/

St. Louis Public Radio

An EF3 tornado on Dec. 10, 2021, flattened half of an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville — killing six people.

Tucked away in the more than 400 bills Illinois lawmakers passed during their spring session is a bill that aims to improve warehouse safety during a tornado**.**

“I was elated,” said Rep. Katie Stuart, D-Edwardsville, who authored the bill, which stems from the Edwardsville tornado that killed six people in 2021.

The [legislation](https://www.ilga.gov/legislation/BillStatus.asp?DocNum=2987&GAID=18&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=161237&SessionID=114&GA=104), which awaits the governor's signature, mandates that all warehouses in the state craft a tornado safety plan and build storm shelters in newly constructed warehouses. It requires county and city building inspectors hold a certification from the International Code Council.

The passage of the legislation in the last hours of the Illinois legislature’s spring session marks a critical step in a more than three-year-long journey to passing legislation in response to the tornado that flattened half of an Amazon warehouse.

The ideas for the legislation were largely crafted in a task force state lawmakers created to study warehouse safety that [concluded late last year](https://www.stlpr.org/government-politics-issues/2024-12-18/illinois-warehouse-safety-task-force-finalizes-report-wants-tornado-shelters-required).

The family of [Clayton Cope](https://www.riverbender.com/news/details/clay-copes-death-in-amazon-warehouse-tornado-incident-leaves-huge-void-forever-for-his-close-friend-group-55372.cfm), one of the six people killed by the tornado, became regular attendees of task force meetings and advocated for the bill’s passage.

“The wife and I are very excited that it has passed, and we're hopeful the governor will sign it. We’ll be ecstatic if he does,” said Lynn Cope, Clayton’s father. “It's a wonderful step forward.”

    ![Image 5: State Rep. Katie Stuart (D-Edwardsville) speaks about her time as a professor on Thursday, April 6, 2023, during a press conference about higher education funding at the Southern Illinois University Edwardsville campus in Edwardsville.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8c62a59/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x2000+0+0/resize/880x587!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Ff4%2F3e%2F48130fca46d59c79b24877470143%2F040623-bm-siue-7.jpg)

Brian Munoz

/

St. Louis Public Radio

Illinois state Rep. Katie Stuart, D-Edwardsville, served on the task force that studied warehouse safety over the last two years.

What's in the bill?
-------------------

The safety plan requires all warehouse operators to prepare a tornado safety plan within 120 days of the bill being signed into law or no later than seven days after a new warehouse becomes operational.

Plans must be specific to the warehouse, reviewed or updated once per year, and should coordinate with the relevant local first responders and disaster agencies.

This requirement stems from the findings of an [investigation](https://www.osha.gov/news/newsreleases/region5/04262022) from the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration that followed the 2021 storm, which [concluded](https://www.stlpr.org/government-politics-issues/2022-04-26/osha-finds-amazon-didnt-violate-federal-rules-in-light-of-the-edwardsville-warehouse-collapse) that some workers at the Amazon warehouse did not remember participating in tornado drills and others didn’t know where to take cover.

For warehouse safety proponents, the OSHA findings show that the warehouses need a storm safety plan.

“We want to make sure that we guarantee that there is one,” Stuart said.

This bill also mandates warehouses constructed after the bill is signed into law meet a “life safety performance level” to handle extreme weather events. In other words, warehouses must have a space to shelter from the expected weather and other types of natural disasters that could happen, Stuart said.

“You can have all the plans you want, but if you don't have a safe place to go, they don't do any good,” she said.

While it was eventually recommended, requiring storm shelters had been a [sticking point](https://www.stlpr.org/government-politics-issues/2024-12-03/illinois-warehouses-should-be-built-with-storm-shelters-state-task-force-recommends) during the task force meetings, as some argued more stringent requirements could force businesses to leave Illinois.

Lawmakers amended the bill, however, to only make requirements applicable for buildings that have regular activity — and not storage facilities or grain elevators, Stuart said.

Some may argue this bill doesn’t mandate enough changes, like requiring storm shelters be built in all warehouses.

“I wouldn’t say I’m done with this work, and I will continue,” Stuart said. “This was a step that we got to take this year, and it's moving us in the right direction.”

The third portion of the bill will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. It amends Illinois’ county and municipal code to require building inspectors hold a certification from International Code Council, the nonprofit trade organization that oversees building safety. Previously, a certification from the council was not required.

    ![Image 6: The Illinois State Capitol on Wednesday, Feb. 15, 2023, in Springfield, Ill.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf173a4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x2000+0+0/resize/880x587!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Ff7%2F9e%2F43bc04f54659ad3e8338cdf658a1%2F021523-bm-capitol-il-1.jpg)

Brian Munoz

/

St. Louis Public Radio

The Illinois state Capitol in February 2023 in Springfield

The final bill enjoyed bipartisan support, passing 51-2 in the Senate and 99-15 in the House.

“It’s one of those things where you hope it will never happen again, but you do have to be prepared,” said Rep. Amy Elik, R-Godfrey, whose district encompasses the Amazon warehouse that was destroyed and [reopened last year](https://www.stlpr.org/economy-business/2024-09-17/edwardsville-amazon-warehouse-ravaged-by-2021-tornado-that-killed-6-has-reopened).

The May 16 tornado that ripped from St. Louis County through north St. Louis, killing five people, followed an [eerily similar trajectory](https://x.com/NWSStLouis/status/1924228335590162776) to the 2021 tornado in the Metro East.

Four days later, the day the House took its first vote on the bill, Illinois lawmakers sheltered in the basement in the Capitol when a tornado warning was issued near Springfield. Both scenarios served as a reminder of this bill’s necessity, lawmakers said.

“It’s not a sexy topic, talking about building codes and what you’re going to require in some of these warehouses,” said Rep. Jay Hoffman, D-Swansea. “But Stuart’s work and the work of the whole task force…I think they came up with a good result.”

For the Cope family, the bill’s passage is a sign that things can get better.

“It helps us — gives us some closure,” Lynn Cope said. “It just helps in the healing process. It really does. Maybe this will help someone in the future. I don’t know. You’ll never know. I just hope it does. That’s all we can ever hope for.”

Gov. JB Pritzker’s office said he will review the legislation.

(TNS) — Deon January had a message for Amazon on Tuesday: You failed to protect her son and five others who died in a tornado at an Amazon warehouse in Edwardsville in December.

January spoke during a news conference hosted by her attorneys, who last month filed a wrongful-death lawsuit on behalf of her late son, 28-year-old DeAndre Morrow. The lawsuit is against Amazon and the companies that oversaw construction of the warehouse damaged by the tornado.

"Amazon had plenty, plenty of time to alert everyone and they failed to do that and they need to be held responsible," January said.

As she cried talking about DeAndre, she was comforted by her husband, Jerrett, and her daughter, Jerriah.

"It's difficult, day by day as a Mom," January said.

"It's not OK. It's not OK."

January said her son wanted to open businesses such as coin laundries and car washes. He wanted to help the homeless.

Amazon released a statement last week that defends the company's actions.

"The tornado that hit our delivery station was extreme and very sudden, with winds that were much like the force of a category 4 hurricane, and we believe our team did the right thing, moving people to shelter as soon as the warning was issued," according to an email from Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel.

"The storm in Edwardsville last fall was a tragedy and our teams on the ground continue to support our employees and the broader community as they work to recover," Nantel said.

Along with January, the other speakers in the news conference at Mount Joy Baptist Church in Edwardsville included one of her attorneys, Ben Crump — who is known nationally for representing George Floyd's family in Minneapolis — and delivery drivers who survived the tornado.

They criticized Amazon's actions before the tornado and since.

"People died because you put profit over safety," said Crump of Tallahassee, Florida.

As a companion to the wrongful-death lawsuit, an emotional distress lawsuit has been filed on behalf of four drivers who survived the tornado against Amazon and the companies that oversaw the construction of the warehouse.

Other plaintiffs are expected to be added to the lawsuit, according to Jennifer Hightower, one of the lawyers for the plaintiffs.

Morrow and five others died when the warehouse walls and roof collapsed in an EF3 tornado packing winds of up to 150 mph at about 8:27 p.m. on Dec. 10. The 1.1 million-square-foot building was on Gateway Commerce Drive near the intersection of Interstate 255 and Interstate 270.

### Amazon Drivers Recall Night of Tornado

A driver who survived the tornado, Jamarco Hickman, 32, of Godfrey, is one of the plaintiffs who spoke Tuesday.

Hickman described that night of the tornado:

"Hearing those walls collapse. The sounds of the loud roar of the tornado, when it slammed into our building. And you just don't know, anything could fly at you.

"My fear of death, I could just not put into words. I was terrified. My co-workers were terrified."

Hickman said he has not received any assistance since the tornado. He lost his job and his 2015 Hyundai Elantra was totaled by the walls that collapsed at the warehouse.

Teresa Haley, president of the NAACP of Illinois, said she hopes someone hearing Hickman's story will donate a car to him.

Hickman said he has suffered financially and mentally since the tornado and that he is getting counseling because he is depressed.

The Edwardsville Community Foundation received a $1 million donation from Amazon the day after the tornado, but a representative from the group could not be reached for comment on Tuesday about how the money is being used.

Another driver, Jada Williams, 26, of Glen Carbon said she rushed back to the warehouse after hearing from her cousin about tornado warnings.

"As soon as I put the van in park, the building just started falling down," Williams said. "I honestly thought the building was going to keep falling."

Williams says she now has trouble getting sleep.

"It's like every time I try to go to sleep, I jump up and think about what happened in the building," she said.

### Amazon Warehouse Didn't Have Storm Shelter

Crump said Morrow's family and the surviving drivers are like "little Davids" going against the "Goliath" of Amazon.

"You are wrong, Amazon, and we have to speak truth to power," Crump said. "Amazon is one of the most powerful entities in the world and these families, these victims, with the community here in Edwardsville" are standing up to the company.

Crump said he found it ironic that you can buy a storm shelter on Amazon's website but the retail giant didn't have one in the Edwardsville warehouse. He noted that two people also died in an Amazon warehouse in a tornado in Baltimore in 2018.

Crump said he and the plaintiff attorneys are representing those "who were tragically affected and injured in that catastrophe that happened here in Edwardsville that we believe was completely preventable if Amazon lived up to its words. And those word's were, 'We aim to be Earth's safest place to work. We are committed to the safety and well being of all Amazon employees every day.'

"But that wasn't true on Dec. 10."

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration last week announced that it would not issue a citation against Amazon because the retail giant "met minimal federal safety guidelines for storm sheltering."

OSHA said it recommends Amazon make the following changes:

— "Ensure that all employees are provided training and participate in emergency weather drills.

— Include site-specific information in severe weather emergency plans.

— All audible warning devices and locations of the device should be clearly identified in the severe weather emergency plan and readily accessible."

OSHA said its investigation showed that a megaphone at the Edwardsville warehouse was locked in a cage at the time of the tornado and was not accessible. Instead, managers verbally told workers to go to a bathroom in the building.

Crump said OSHA made a "scathing" report of Amazon's actions.

"And that report completely contradicted Amazon's statement about being the safest place on Earth for employees to work and that their employees are their most valuable commodity," he said.

A previous wrongful-death lawsuit was filed earlier this year on behalf of Alice and Randy McEwen, the parents of 26-year-old Austin McEwen, who died in the tornado.

The four others who died in the tornado are Clayton Lynn Cope, 29, of Alton; Etheria S. Hebb, 34, of St. Louis; Larry E. Virden, 46, of Collinsville; and Kevin D. Dickey, 62, of Carlyle.

**AIDE-MEMOIRE** **TANZANIA FOOD SYSTEMS RESILIENCE PROGRAM (P179818, Cr. 7331-TZ)** **Implementation Support Mission, April 2 - 10, 2025** **I.** **Introduction** 1. A World Bank (WB) mission met with the representatives of the Government of Tanzania (GoT) to carry out the fourth Implementation Support Mission for the Tanzania Food Systems Resilience Program (TFSRP) during April 2-10, 2025. The mission would like to express its appreciation to the representatives of the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) on the mainland; and the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation, Natural Resources and Livestock (MAINL) in Zanzibar. The lists of officials and WB mission members are included in Annex 2. 2. The main objective of the mission was to support the implementation of the Program in five areas: (i) evaluate the overall progress of the operation’s implementation in mainland and Zanzibar including procurement, financial management, and environmental and social safeguards; (ii) review the delivery status of the Program Action Plan; (iii) assess the verification of results for the Program-for-Results Financing Program; (iv) evaluate the progress of the repurposing agenda through soil health smart subsidy funded through the FS2030 Multi-Donor Trust Fund; (v) review progress and discuss co-financing with the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). 3. This aide-memoire records the major findings of the mission and agreements reached between the GoT and the WB team.
