The construction and safety standards , specifically , are at 24 C.F.R. Part 3280.") The MHCSS, sometimes referred to as the "HUD Code," are issued by HUD and established under the authority of the National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974, as amended (42 U.S.C. §§5401-5426). The purposes of the law include protecting the quality, durability, safety, and affordability of manufactured homes and providing for the establishment of uniform standards for manufactured homes.[128](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn128 "42 U.S.C. §5401.") A uniform standard may reduce the costs and burdens to manufacturers of ensuring compliance with multiple different codes, since manufactured homes constructed in one state may be shipped to other states to be installed. HUD's development of the MHCSS was informed by existing model codes and standards,[129](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn129 "In particular, the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards (MHCSS) drew substantially from the existing National Fire Protection Association Standards for manufactured homes. The 1975 MHCSS proposed rule noted that HUD determined that the mo st appropriate course of action ... would be to develop a complete Federal standard covering mobile home construction and safety rather than adopt, by reference, all or part of the standards or codes for mobile homes currently...") and updates to the MHCSS may take into account existing codes and standards.[130](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn130 "For example, a HUD regulatory impact analysis prepared in relation to a 2021 final rule that amended the MHCSS noted that some of the amendments were made \"to remain on par with several aspects of the International Residential Code (IRC), which serves as the basis for state and local building codes. Updates based on the IRC are generally safety-based and ensure manufactured homes contain the same or similar safety standards as site-built homes.\" See HUD, Regulatory Impact Analysis of FR-614...") Many MHCSS requirements refer to existing codes and standards that are incorporated _by reference_.[131](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn131 "By reference generally means that a certain number of copies (typically one) of the codes or standards must be maintained by a government entity (typically a printed copy available at one or more specified building department offices). See for example, UT Municipal Technical Advisory, \"Building Codes Adopted by Reference,\" https://www.mtas.tennessee.edu/reference/adopting-building-codes-reference . See 24 C.F.R. §3280.4 for how HUD incorporates by reference.")

The MHCSS address various aspects of manufactured home construction, including planning and design; fire safety; body and frame construction; testing; thermal protection; plumbing systems; heating, cooling, and fuel burning systems; electrical systems; and transportation. Although HUD issues the MHCSS, DOE is directed by law to set energy conservation standards for manufactured homes (see the "[What Energy Efficiency Standards Apply to Manufactured Housing?](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref141975329)" section). The MHCSS preempt state and local requirements, meaning states and local governments cannot set different standards related to any aspect of manufactured housing performance addressed by the MHCSS.[132](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn132 "42 U.S.C. § 5403(d) .") HUD updates the MHCSS periodically with input from the Manufactured Housing Consensus Committee, which includes members representing manufactured housing producers or retailers, consumers, and general interest and public officials.[133](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn133 "The Manufactured Housing Consensus Committee is established in statute at 42 U.S.C. 5403(a)(3).")

In 2000, Congress amended the statute to direct HUD to establish the Model Manufactured Home Installation Standards,[134](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn134 "42 U.S.C. §5404 .") which went into effect in 2008.[135](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn135 "HUD , \" Model Manufactured Home Installation Standards, \" 72 Federal Register 59337-59395, October 19, 2007, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2007/10/19/07-5004/model-manufactured-home-installation-standards . The model installation standards are at 24 C . F . R . P art 3285.") Unlike the MHCSS, the Model Manufactured Home Installation Standards do not preempt state requirements. Rather, they establish minimum standards for the installation of manufactured homes, but states can set installation requirements that exceed the Model Manufactured Home Installation Standards.[136](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn136 "For HUD's discussion of public comments received related to the Model Manufactured Home Installation Standards and preemption, see HUD's final rule promulgating the model installation standards at 72 Federal Register 59338.")

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)While HUD issues the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards, DOE is required to establish energy efficiency standards for manufactured housing under Section 413 of the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA; [P.L. 110-140](https://www.congress.gov/bill/110th-congress/house-bill/6/text)). EISA directs that, after notice and opportunity for comment by manufacturers and other interested parties and after consultation with HUD, DOE uses the most recent version of the International Energy Conservation Code (IECC), including supplements, except when the Secretary finds that the code is not cost-effective or that "a more stringent standard would be more cost-effective, based upon the impact of the code on the purchase price of manufactured housing and on total life-cycle construction and operating costs." The energy efficiency standards are to be updated not later than one year after any revision to the IECC.

Section 413 of EISA also provides for enforcement. Any manufacturer that violates the energy efficiency standards is liable for a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed 1% of the manufacturer's retail list price of the manufactured housing.

DOE published a final rule establishing these standards in May 2022.[137](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn137 "DOE , \" Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Manufactured Housing, \" 87 Federal Register 32728-32824, May 31, 2022, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/05/31/2022-10926/energy-conservation-program-energy-conservation-standards-for-manufactured-housing .") The compliance date for the rule was scheduled to be May 31, 2023; however, on May 30, 2023, DOE issued a final rule delaying compliance "to allow DOE more time to establish enforcement procedures that provide clarity for manufacturers and other stakeholders regarding DOE's expectations of manufacturers and DOE's plans for enforcing the standards."[138](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn138 "DOE , \"Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Manufactured Housing ; Extension of Compliance Date, \" 8 8 Federal Register 34411-34419 , May 3 0 , 202 3.") The compliance date was extended to July 1, 2025, for multi-section manufactured homes and until 60 days after DOE issues enforcement procedures for single-section manufactured homes. DOE published a notice of proposed rulemaking to establish enforcement procedures on December 26, 2023, with a comment period that closed on February 26, 2024.[139](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn139 "DOE, \" Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Manufactured Housing; Enforcement ,\" 88 Federal Register 88844 -88854, December 26, 2023.")

The federal government supports the development and maintenance of housing through a range of programs and activities, including grants, loans, mortgage insurance, rental assistance, and tax credits. These programs may support new construction, rehabilitation, or acquisition of housing. HUD administers many of these programs, but some are administered by other federal agencies.

In general, the federal government requires housing that is newly constructed or substantially rehabilitated under most federal programs to meet one of the nationally recognized model building codes or a state or local building code that meets standards set by the relevant federal agency (such as being based on a nationally recognized model building code).[140](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn140 "Although federal programs that support the acquisition of a property or provide rental subsidies to an existing property generally also involve minimum quality standards, this section focuses on programs supporting new construction or substantial rehabilitation.") Federal programs may have additional requirements beyond SLTT codes and standards or the model building codes for property durability, accessibility, fire safety, energy efficiency, and broadband readiness that are established by federal laws and regulations.

For example, HUD has adopted Minimum Property Standards (MPS) that apply to newly constructed housing under certain programs (see text box "HUD's Minimum Property Standards"). Some of the MPS requirements may exceed SLTT codes and standards, such as minimum durability requirements for items such as doors, windows, gutters, kitchen cabinets, and carpeting intended to ensure HUD-assisted or Federal Housing Administration (FHA)-insured housing does not lose value because of deterioration of these items.

Other federal requirements that may apply include certain government-wide requirements applicable to federal buildings and programs, including, but not limited to, federally related housing. These include certain accessibility requirements (e.g., Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 ([P.L. 93-112](https://www.congress.gov/bill/93rd-congress/house-bill/8070/text) and the ADA) and fire safety requirements (e.g., sprinkler systems, smoke detectors). Other laws or regulations establish requirements that apply to multiple housing programs within or across agencies, such as HUD requirements related to broadband readiness,[141](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn141 "In 2016, HUD finalized a rule requiring the installation of broadband infrastructure in all HUD-funded new construction and substantial rehabilitation of multifamily housing. This requirement does not apply to properties that only receive HUD-insured financing (through a Federal Housing Administration - insured mortgage) but does apply to most major HUD grant-funded programs, including public housing, the Community Development Block Grant program, the HOME Investment Partnerships P rogram, ho...") carbon monoxide detector requirements,[142](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn142 "Recently enacted laws have expanded federal requirements related to carbon monoxide detectors in federally assisted housing. See the Carbon Monoxide Alarms Leading Every Resident t o Safety Act of 2019 , enacted in Section 101 of Title I of Division Q of P.L. 116-260 .") and energy efficiency requirements.[143](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn143 "The Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA, P.L. 110-140 ) amended the Cranston-Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act of 1990 to require HUD and the U.S. Department of Agriculture ( USDA ) to adopt energy efficiency standards for newly constructed housing under certain programs. It also included provisions related to adopting revisions to those standards . (See 42 U.S.C. §12709.) In April 2024, HUD and USDA published updated standards in the Federal Register , ado...") Finally, certain program-specific property standards may apply, as discussed for specific examples below.

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)HUD's Minimum Property Standards

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) established and maintains Minimum Property Standards (MPS) that apply to buildings constructed under HUD housing programs, including new single-family and multifamily housing insured with Federal Housing Administration (FHA) financing and low-rent public housing.

Until the mid-1980s, HUD maintained separate MPS for different types of structures. Today, HUD instead generally accepts model building codes and their reference standards or state, local, tribal, or territorial building codes deemed acceptable by the HUD Secretary as fulfilling the requirements of MPS. Additionally, HUD has adopted into MPS standards that go beyond those found in model building codes. These include durability standards for items including, but not limited to, doors, windows, gutters and downspouts, painting and wall covers, kitchen cabinets, and carpeting.

HUD's MPS can be found in _Minimum Property Standards for Housing, 1994 Edition_, HUD Handbook 4910.1, https://www.hud.gov/hudclips/handbooks/housing-4910-1.MPS regulations can be found at 24 C.F.R. 200 Subpart S. For more information, see HUD, "MPS Supplementing Model Building Codes," https://www.hud.gov/hud-partners/minimum-property-standards-resources.

v/crs-product/R47665)What Building Codes Apply to Federal Mortgage Insurance and Loan Programs?

Multiple federal agencies—HUD's FHA, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Rural Housing Service—provide mortgage insurance, loan guarantees, or direct loans for single-family or multifamily housing. In addition to complying with applicable SLTT building codes and standards, properties securing mortgages made by one of these entities also must comply with certain requirements set by the respective agency backing the mortgage. In addition to ensuring housing financed with these mortgages is safe for residents, these property standards are intended to ensure the housing is of sufficient quality to protect the agency's financial interests.

v/crs-product/R47665)What Building Codes Apply to Federal Grant and Tax Credit Programs?

In addition to loans and mortgage insurance, the federal government provides support for affordable housing development via grants and tax credits. Examples of federal requirements applicable to various affordable housing programs are provided below.

*   The HOME Investment Partnerships Program provides formula grants to states and localities that they can use for various affordable housing purposes. Although the specific requirements vary depending on the type of activity, in general, the housing must meet all applicable state and local codes, ordinances, and requirements (or, in the absence of local building codes, the International Residential Code (IRC), International Building Code (IBC), or International Existing Building Code (IEBC)).[144](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn144 "HOME property standards are at 24 C.F.R. §92.251.") For rental housing assisted with HOME funds, the jurisdictions administering the funds must establish ongoing property standards that apply for the duration of the affordability period and conduct periodic inspections throughout the affordability period.[145](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn145 "24 C.F.R. §92.251(f) and 24 C.F.R. §92.504(d). The minimum required affordability periods for HOME-assisted rental housing range from 5 to 20 years, depending on the type of activity and the amount of HOME funds invested. See 24 C.F.R. §92.252(e).")
*   Another HUD formula grant program, the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), provides funding to states and localities that can be used for a range of community development activities, including certain housing-related activities such as housing rehabilitation. Unlike HOME, there is no federal requirement for housing that is rehabilitated using CDBG funds to meet applicable state and local codes, although jurisdictions may set such requirements.[146](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn146 "HUD, HOME and CDBG Guidebook , February 2012, p p . 31 and 63 , https://files.hudexchange.info/resources/documents/HOME-CDBGGuidebook.pdf .")
*   In response to certain disasters, Congress sometimes provides supplemental appropriations under CDBG authorities for long-term disaster recovery (CDBG-DR) and mitigation activities (CDBG-MIT). CDBG-DR and CDBG-MIT are not formally authorized, and rulemaking may vary in different disaster responses. HUD typically has required CDBG-DR grantees to describe, in their action plans, how they plan to support the adoption and enforcement of modern and/or resilient building codes that mitigate against natural hazard risks, including climate-related risks.[147](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn147 "For example, see HUD, \"Allocations for Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery and Implementation of the CDBG-DR Consolidated Waivers and Alternative Requirements Notice,\" 87 Federal Register 6364-6392, February 3, 2022, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2022/02/03/2022-02209/allocations-for-community-development-block-grant-disaster-recovery-and-implementation-of-the . See also CRS Report R46475, The Community Development Block Grant's Disaster Recovery (CDBG-D...") HUD also has required that CDBG-MIT grantees describe plans to follow the latest edition of published disaster-resistant model building codes and standards (which could include the International Code Council's wildland urban interface codes as well as American Society of Civil Engineers flood resistant standards (ASCE 24) and many hazard minimum loading standards (ASCE 7), see "[Model Building Codes](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref144134756)" and "[Standards](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref144125538)" sections).[148](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn148 "HUD, \"Allocations, Common Application, Waivers, and Alternative Requirements for Community Development Block Grant Mitigation Grantees,\" 84 Federal Register 45838-45871, August 30, 2019, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/08/30/2019-18607/allocations-common-application-waivers-and-alternative-requirements-for-community-development-block .")
*   Public housing is a form of affordable rental housing owned by local public housing authorities but funded by grants from, and governed by contracts with, the federal government. When federally funded public housing properties are being newly developed or redeveloped, they must meet HUD's Minimum Property Standards (see text box above). After public housing is constructed, it is subject to periodic inspection by HUD inspectors, which evaluate the housing against HUD-established minimum quality standards.[149](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn149 "The current standards are called the Uniform Physical Condition Standards (UPCS). See HUD, \"Uniform Physical Condition Standards and Physical Inspection,\" 63 Federal Register 46565-46850, September 1, 1998. HUD is in the process of adopting new standards to replace UPCS, referred to as the National Standards for the Physical Inspection of Real Estate (NSPIRE) standards. For more information, see HUD, \"The Building of a New Inspection Model - National Standards for the Physical Inspection...") These periodic inspections are intended to ensure HUD-assisted housing is decent, safe, sanitary, and in good repair.
*   The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) program provides federal tax credits that developers can use to subsidize the development, rehabilitation, or acquisition of affordable rental housing. The program is administered by the Department of the Treasury, and its regulations require that, to qualify for credits under the LIHTC program, a property must be suitable for occupancy, taking into account local health, safety, and building codes.[150](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn150 "Treas. Reg. §1.42-5(c) (1) (vi).") State agencies are required to physically inspect LIHTC properties periodically throughout the program's 15-year compliance window. [](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)Communities that participate in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) must adopt minimum floodplain management standards, which are set forth in regulations,[152](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn152 "See 44 C.F.R. Part 60, particularly 44 C.F.R. §60.3.") to participate in the NFIP.[153](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn153 "42 U.S.C. §4022(a)(1). See also CRS Report R47612, Building Resilience: FEMA's Building Codes Policies and Considerations for Congress , by Diane P. Horn and Erica A. Lee .") Though the standards appear in federal regulations, the standards have the force of law only because they are adopted and enforced by a state or local government. These standards are minimum requirements for NFIP participation; states and communities can elect to adopt higher standards as a means of mitigating flood risk. NFIP minimum standards include, among many other conditions, that communities (1) require permits for development in Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs);[154](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn154 "FEMA defines the Special Flood Hazard Area as an area with a 1% or greater risk of flooding every year.") (2) require elevation of the lowest floor of all new residential buildings in the SFHA to be at or above Base Flood Elevation;[155](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn155 "FEMA defines Base Flood Elevation (BFE) as the water-surface elevation of the base flood, which is the 1%-annual-chance flood, commonly called the 100-year flood. The probability is 1% that rising water will reach BFE height in any given year.") (3) restrict development in the regulatory floodway to prevent increasing the risk of flooding; and (4) require certain construction materials and methods that minimize future flood damage.[156](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn156 "44 C.F.R. §60 .3.") These requirements apply to new construction in the SFHA. In addition, when improvements to existing buildings meet the definition of _substantial improvement_,[157](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn157 "4 4 C.F.R . § 59.1 defines substantial improvement as any reconstruction, rehabilitation, addition, or other improvement of a structure, the cost of which equals or exceeds 50% of the market value of the structure before the \"start of construction\" of the improvement. This term includes structures that have incurred \"substantial damage,\" regardless of the actual repair work performed. Floodplain management requirements for new construction apply to substantial improvements.") or when damage meets the definition of _substantial damage_,[158](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn158 "4 4 C.F.R . §5 9.1 defines substantial damage as damage of any origin sustained by a structure whereby the cost of restoring the structure to its before - damaged condition would equal or exceed 50% of the market value of the structure before the damage occurred.") communities must enforce the requirements to bring those structures into compliance with the minimum standards for new construction. FEMA has produced guidance summarizing the flood-resistant provisions of the 2021 International Code Council codes and American Society of Civil Engineers flood resistant standards (ASCE 24-14) that represent higher standards than NFIP requirements (see "[Standards](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref144125721)" section).[159](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn159 "FEMA, Building Code Requirements That Exceed or Are More Specific Than the National Flood Insurance Program , May 2021, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_building-code-exceed-nfip-complete_2021.pdf .") It also has provided a summary of the flood-resistant provisions of the 2024 international codes.[160](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn160 "FEMA, Flood-Resistant Provisions of the 2024 International Codes , https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema-flood-provisions-2024-international-codes.pdf .")

The Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (Stafford Act, [P.L. 100-707](https://www.congress.gov/bill/100th-congress/house-bill/2707/text)), federal regulations, and FEMA policy generally require recipients of federal assistance to comply with applicable building codes when conducting federally funded construction projects. In particular, FEMA programs that provide funding for hazard mitigation require resilient rebuilding.[161](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn161 "CRS Report R47612, Building Resilience: FEMA's Building Codes Policies and Considerations for Congress , by Diane P. Horn and Erica A. Lee . For additional information on FEMA hazard mitigation, see CRS Report R46989, FEMA Hazard Mitigation: A First Step Toward Climate Adaptation , by Diane P. Horn .") However, each FEMA grant program includes different code compliance requirements, and FEMA's 2022 _Building Codes Strategy_ announced that the agency's first goal was to align building code policies across FEMA programs.[162](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn162 "FEMA, Building Codes Strategy, March 2022, pp. 14-20.") In addition, several FEMA programs may provide financial and technical assistance to SLTTs seeking funding for the adoption of new building codes or the enforcement of existing codes. In November 2024, FEMA released an updated playbook for jurisdictions adopting and enforcing building codes that included an overview on relevant FEMA assistance.[163](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn163 "FEMA, Building Codes Adoption, 2024 .")

Many federal agencies work to inform model building codes that can then be adopted and enforced by SLTT building codes to enhance building performance (e.g., resiliency, efficiency, environmental impact reduction). In addition, federal agencies may incentivize building owners and communities to adopt enhanced model building codes (often beyond the SLTTs building codes) through financial and technical assistance for building construction, operation and maintenance, or repair (see "[Federal Role: Code Requirements](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref141975485)" section).

On June 1 2022, the Biden Administration announced a National Initiative to Advance Building Codes (NIABC); this initiative outlined some federal agency activities to enhance codes.[166](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn166 "The White House, \"Biden-Harris Administration Launches Initiative to Modernize Building Codes, Improve Climate Resilience, and Reduce Energy Costs,\" fact sheet, June 1, 2022, https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/01/fact-sheet-biden-harris-administration-launches-initiative-to-modernize-building-codes-improve-climate-resilience-and-reduce-energy-costs/  .") In general, these activities can be categorized as research and development leading to enhanced model building codes, assisting SLTTs in adopting and enforcing enhanced codes, and expanding the federal government's adoption and enforcement of enhanced codes for federal buildings and military buildings. FEMA's Mitigation Framework Leadership Group stood up the Building Codes Task Force in 2022 to lead the NIABC effort. This task force is to submit annual progress reports to the White House, describing the building code-related activities of individual federal agencies as well as accomplishments of the task force and updated priorities.[167](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn167 "See FEMA, Mitigation Framework Leadership Group Progress Report: National Initiative to Advance Building Codes , December 20, 2022 ; and FEMA, Mitigation Framework Leadership Group Progress Report: National Initiative to Advance Building Codes , December 20, 2023 . The 2022 and 2024 progress report s w ere not available online as of March 31, 2025.")

NIST, FEMA, and DOE have research and development activities to improve building codes.[168](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn168 "CRS Report R47215, Hazard-Resilient Buildings: Sustaining Occupancy and Function After a Natural Disaster , by Linda R. Rowan ; and CRS Report R47612, Building Resilience: FEMA's Building Codes Policies and Considerations for Congress , by Diane P. Horn and Erica A. Lee .") All three agencies also have programs to assist SLTTs in adopting and enforcing improved codes. The CEQ, GSA, DOE, and EPA have activities to enhance codes for federal buildings and military buildings. In particular, the NIABC calls for federal building performance standards developed by these agencies and departments to include a net-zero emissions building portfolio by 2045.[169](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn169 "The White House, \"Biden-Harris Administration Launches Initiative to Modernize Building Codes, Improve Climate Resilience, and Reduce Energy Costs,\" fact sheet, June 1, 2022, https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/06/01/fact-sheet-biden-harris-administration-launches-initiative-to-modernize-building-codes-improve-climate-resilience-and-reduce-energy-costs .")

Role Does the Federal Government Play in Tracking Building Code Adoption and Enforcement?

The federal government tracks the types of building codes in use to understand the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats to building stock in the United States and its territories. For example, FEMA tracks building codes in use by SLTTs and notes that some of these codes include hazard resistant design elements, which may improve a building's ability to withstand a disaster.[170](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn170 "FEMA, \"Nationwide Building Code Adoption Tracking,\" https://www.fema.gov/emergency-managers/risk-management/building-science/bcat . See also FEMA, Building Codes Adoption , 2024 .")

v/crs-product/R47665)What Role Does the Federal Government Play in Copyright Protection for Standards Incorporated by Reference?

Federal and SLTT entities commonly adopt a model building code or a standard from a standards developing organization by incorporating such model codes or standards into law or regulation by reference.[172](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn172 "Hereinafter in this section, model building codes and standards will be referred to as standards .") Other incorporated by reference (IBR) standards may serve as a reference or as a guidance but do not formally impose legal obligations. Federal regulations require that IBR standards in regulations be made "reasonably available to interested parties."[173](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn173 "1 C.F.R. 51.5(b)(2) (2019); 5 U.S.C. 552(a)(1). See also Administrative Conference of the United States \"Incorporation by Reference in the CFR,\" https://www.acus.gov/recommendation/incorporation-reference .") SLTTs may have their own policies regarding access to IBR standards.[174](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn174 "CRS Report R47656, Copyright in Standards Incorporated by Reference into Law and the Pro Codes Act , by Kevin J. Hickey .")

Standards are typically considered original works of authorship entitled to copyright protection.[175](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn175 "17 U.S.C. § 106.") SDOs often sell copies of their standards, in some cases to recoup the cost of developing the standards. Under copyright protection, third parties are prevented from making or distributing unauthorized copies of standards. Many SDOs also may make their standards available in some form online. For decades, federal courts have considered competing legal arguments about the copyright of IBR standards. Third-party organizations have argued that IBR standards lose copyright protection once they are incorporated into law or that they are permitted to publish IBR standards on third-party sites or materials, under the fair use doctrine. Courts have not reached a consensus about copyright protection for IBR standards. Bills considered in the 118 th Congress (the Pro Codes Act, [H.R. 1631](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/1631) and [S. 835](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/senate-bill/835)) would have provided that otherwise copyrightable IBR standards retain their copyright protection even after a government incorporates them into law.[176](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn176 "See also \"Protecting and Enhancing Public Access to Codes Act,\" Congressional Record , daily edition, vol. 170, part 118 (July 23, 2024), https://www.congress.gov/congressional-record/volume-170/issue-118/house-section/article/H4658-1 .") The bills also would have required SDOs to make the IBR standards publicly accessible online in a readable format for free.[177](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn177 "CRS Report R47656, Copyright in Standards Incorporated by Reference into Law and the Pro Codes Act , by Kevin J. Hickey .")

In the past, the U.S. Fire Administration, in FEMA, has provided training on building and fire codes for fire officials, conducted through its National Fire Academy,[178](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn178 "U.S. Fire Administration (USFA), \"On-Campus Courses,\" https://www.usfa.fema.gov/nfa/courses/on-campus/  . On March 7, 2025, FEMA canceled all in-person first responder training courses at the U SFA's National Fire Academy and the Emergency Management Institute , colocated at the National Emergency Training Center in Emmitsburg, MD . The purpose of the cancellation was, according to public reports, to review \"programs and spending to ensure alignment with Administration priorities....") and collected fire incident data through the National Fire Incident Reporting System (recently updated to the National Emergency Response Information System platform). The fire incident data can help with fire science research and assessment of the effectiveness of fire protections measures and fire safety standards.[179](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn179 "USFA, \"National Emergency Response Information System,\" https://www.usfa.fema.gov/nfirs/neris/  .") It also can help in advising fire departments on emerging fire risks (e.g., electric vehicle fires).[180](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn180 "For example, see USFA, \"Electric Vehicle Fire Safety,\" https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/vehicle-fires/electric-vehicles/  .")

In addition, the federal government has prioritized fire standards for equipment and fire systems through federal grants. For example, in the 2024 Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response grant notice, FEMA prioritized funding for NFPA standards-based personal protective clothing and equipment.[181](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn181 "FEMA, \"The Department of Homeland Security Notice of Funding Opportunity Fiscal Year 2024 Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response (SAFER) Grant,\" p. 68, https://www.grants.gov/search-results-detail/352757 .") It also prioritized funding for NFPA-certified training. Further, through the Assistance to Firefighters Grants Program, Fire Prevention and Safety Grants, the federal government funds fire safety education, awareness, and prevention activities. Through firefighter grant programs, Congress has made available over $16 billion since 2001 to fire departments to ensure the safety of firefighters, hire and train new firefighters, and support fire prevention activities.[182](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn182 "CRS Report R48283, Reauthorization of the U.S. Fire Administration and of the Assistance to Firefighters Grant (AFG) and Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response (SAFER) Programs , by Brian E. Humphreys . (See Table A-2 for total funding provided through FEMA firefighter grant programs, including the Assistance to Firefighter Grant and Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response Programs—more than $16 billion.)")

Role Does the Federal Government Play in Strengthening Energy Efficiency?

Two enacted laws provided funding to programs within DOE to expand technical assistance to SLTTs: the [](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA; [P.L. 117-58](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/3684/text)) and [P.L. 117-169](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/5376/text), commonly referred to as the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (IRA). Several actions by the second Trump Administration may have implications for spending on these programs, including the issuance in February 2025 of E.O. 14154, "Unleashing American Energy"; DOE's reported plans to review all post-presidential election awards; and an OMB memorandum (M-25-11, "Guidance Regarding Section 7 of the Executive Order Unleashing American Energy").[183](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn183 "Executive Order 14154, \"Unleashing American Energy,\" 90 Federal Register 8363, January 20, 2025; Peter Behr, \"DOE P roject F unding N eeds Trump L ieutenants' B lessing,\" EnergyWire , February 12, 2025; OMB, \" Guidance Regarding Section 7 of the Executive Order Unleashing American Energy , \" M-25-11, January 21, 2025, https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2025/01/omb-memo-m-25-11/  . A separate OMB memorandum (M-25-13) c ould have paused obligation and disbursement...") Section 7 of E.O. 14154 directs agencies to pause disbursement of funds appropriated in the IIJA and the IRA. E.O. 14154 directs agencies to submit findings to OMB within 90 days of the date of the order, and the executive order further directs agencies not to disburse identified funds until the OMB director and assistant to the President for economic policy have replied. OMB M-25-11 discusses the scope of the pause of IIJA and IRA funds and explains the pause in disbursements applies only to any funding supporting policies at odds with the Trump Administration policies articulated in Section 2 of E.O. 14154. Whether disbursements under existing awards for programs discussed below are covered by E.O. 14154 is uncertain. On March 6, 2025, a federal district court preliminarily enjoined the Trump Administration from enforcing certain directives to pause federal funds under existing awards.[184](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn184 "State of New York et al. v. Donald Trump et al., ( 25-cv-00039-JJM-PAS ), pp. 43-45, https://www.rid.uscourts.gov/state-new-york-et-al-v-trump-et-al-25-cv-00039-jjm-pas .")

Section 40511 of the IIJA added a Section 309 to the Energy Conservation and Production Act ([P.L. 94-385](https://www.congress.gov/bill/94th-congress/house-bill/12169/text)). The section establishes within DOE a competitive grant program for state building code agencies (or other eligible entities) to enable sustained cost-effective implementation of updated building energy codes. The program is to consider factors such as prospective energy savings, long-term sustainability of those savings, prospective benefits (including resilience and peak load reduction, occupant safety and health, and environmental performance), demonstrated capacity of the agency/eligible entity, and the need for assistance. Eligible activities include creating/enabling partnerships for training builders, contractors, architects, designers, construction professionals, and building code officials; collecting and disseminating quantitative data; developing and implementing plans (including measuring compliance); addressing implementation needs for rural, suburban, and urban areas; and implementing updates in energy codes.

Section 50131 of the IRA provided funding to DOE for two types of technical assistance grants to SLTTs for building energy codes development and implementation. The law established two grant programs to assist state and local governments with building energy codes. One program is intended to assist with the adoption of the latest residential or commercial building energy codes and implementation of a plan to achieve full compliance with codes. For residential buildings, the latest building energy code equivalent would be the 2024 International Energy Conservation Code. For commercial buildings, the latest building energy standard would be the 2019 Standard 90.1. The second program is intended to assist with the adoption of residential or commercial building energy codes that meet or exceed the zero-energy provisions of the 2021 IECC or equivalent _stretch code_ and implementation of a plan to achieve full compliance with codes.[185](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn185 "A stretch code is a locally mandated code or alternative compliance path that is more aggressive than the base energy code, resulting in buildings that achieve higher energy savings. New Buildings Institute, \"Stretch Codes,\" https://newbuildings.org/code_policy/utility-programs-stretch-codes/stretch-codes/      .")

Other Safety Systems (Non-Fire) May Apply to Federal Buildings?

At the direction of Congress, HHS and GSA jointly have developed voluntary safety station standards for federal facilities. These standards, which are promulgated in [_GSA Bulletin FMR-C-2024-01_](https://www.gsa.gov/system/files/Safety%20Station%20FMR%20Bulletin%20C-2024-01%20%282%29.pdf), recommend that agencies include three major components in their safety stations: (1) automated external defibrillators to assist individuals experiencing sudden cardiac arrest; (2) opioid reversal agents, such as Nalaxone, which can reverse an opioid overdose; and (3) hemorrhagic control kits to control bleeding due to injury.[186](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn186 "GSA, Safety Station Program Guidelines in Federal Facilities , GSA B ulletin FMR C–2024–01, December 21, 2023. https://www.gsa.gov/system/files/Safety%20Station%20FMR%20Bulletin%20C-2024-01%20%282%29.pdf .") The standards recommend that agencies offer training programs to their employees on proper use of each of the three components.

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)What Role Does the Federal Government Play in Strengthening Hazard Resistance and Resilience?

FEMA and NIST conduct research on hazard resistant model building codes.[187](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn187 "CRS Report R47215, Hazard-Resilient Buildings: Sustaining Occupancy and Function After a Natural Disaster , by Linda R. Rowan ; and CRS Report R47612, Building Resilience: FEMA's Building Codes Policies and Considerations for Congress , by Diane P. Horn and Erica A. Lee .") NIST's Buildings and Construction Program develops safety standards for construction and studies ways to better protect buildings from hazards such as earthquakes and windstorms.[188](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn188 "NIST, \"Buildings and Construction,\" https://www.nist.gov/buildings-construction .") FEMA's Building Science Branch studies how natural hazards affect structures and works with industry professionals to enhance structures' hazard resistance.[189](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn189 "FEMA, \"Building Science,\" https://www.fema.gov/emergency-managers/risk-management/building-science .") These and other federal agencies may submit model building code proposals to standards developing organizations, such as the International Code Council and the American Society of Civil Engineers, to enhance model codes and standards to be more resistant to specific hazards.

In addition, Congress has directed NIST and FEMA to take other actions that may contribute to the development of earthquake-resistant buildings (42 U.S.C. §7704).The 2018 reauthorization of the National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program also defined _community resilience_ as "the ability of a community to prepare and plan for, absorb, recover from, and more successfully adapt to adverse seismic events" (42 U.S.C. §7703) and directed NIST to conduct research to "improve community resilience through building codes and standards" (42 U.S.C. §7704(b)(5)).[190](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn190 "CRS Report R43141, The National Earthquake Hazards Reduction Program (NEHRP): Overview and Issues for Congress , by Linda R. Rowan .") More broadly, FEMA defined _community resilience_ as "the ability of a community to prepare for anticipated natural hazards, adapt to changing conditions, and withstand and recover rapidly from disruptions."[191](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn191 "FEMA, National Risk Index: Community Resilience , https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/community-resilience .")

Role Does the Federal Government Play in Identifying and Assessing Natural Hazard Risks?

FEMA, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), among other federal agencies, observe, monitor, model, and in some cases forecast natural hazards, including those that may affect buildings and their occupants. These agencies often provide hazard assessments to help to define where hazard risks are high for people and property in the United States. FEMA developed a National Risk Index (NRI),[192](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn192 "FEMA, \" National Risk Index for Natural Hazards ,\" https://www.fema.gov/flood-maps/products-tools/national-risk-index .") an online mapping application that identifies communities most at risk from 18 natural hazards at the county and census tract levels and maps a community's social vulnerability, community resilience, and other environmental factors ([**Figure 5**](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref144193435)). The NRI provide s a baseline relative risk measurement for each county and census tract in the United States. The NRI shows a score for each individual hazard as well as a composite score for all 18 natural hazards. The most recent update of the NRI was in March 2023 and included NRI scores for all of the U.S. territories.[193](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn193 "FEMA, \" National Risk Index Data Version and Update Documentation , \" March 2023, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_national-risk-index-data-version-and-update-documentation.pdf .") For tribal nations, the NRI has data resources available to help identify the spatial relationships between tribal land area representation and the NRI data.[194](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn194 "FEMA, \" National Risk Index Frequently Asked Questions, Which Parts of the United States Are Included in the National Risk Index? ,\" https://hazards.fema.gov/nri/frequently-asked-questions#which-parts-of-the-united-states-are-included-in-the-nri .")

The Community Disaster Resilience Zones Act of 2022 ([P.L. 117-141](https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/3579/text)) amended the Stafford Act to require the President to maintain and update a natural hazard assessment program that develops and maintains publicly available products to show the risk of natural hazards across the United States. The act also required the President to identify and designate Community Disaster Resilience Zones (CDRZs) that identify disadvantaged communities most at risk of natural hazards. Designated communities are to hold the CDRZ designation for five years.[195](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn195 "Community Disaster Resilience Zones are defined in P.L. 117-255 as the 50 census tracts assigned the highest individual hazard risk ratings. The individual risk ratings reflect (1) an intersection of (a) loss to population equivalence, (b) building value, and (c) agricultural value; (2) high social vulnerability ratings and low community resilience ratings; and (3) any other elements determined by the President. See 42 U.S.C. §5136(d).") The President is authorized to increase the federal cost share for pre-disaster mitigation funding to CDRZs to not more than 90% of the total cost of the mitigation project.[196](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn196 "42 U.S.C. §5136(g).") FEMA used the NRI and the Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool to identify the most at-risk and in-need communities.[197](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn197 "On Jan uary 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 14148 rescinding President Biden's Executive Order 14008, which established the Justice40 Initiative and required CEQ to create a Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool . The tool is no longer available. Harvard, \"Rollback: Climate Economic Justice Screening Tool (CEJST) Removed,\" https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/tracker/ceqs-climate-economic-justice-screening-tool-removed/  . Executive Order 14148 of January 20, 2025, \"...") FEMA announced the first 483 CDRZs in September 2023, in all 50 states and the District of Columbia. In November 2024 and January 2025, an additional 231 census tracts were designated on tribal nations and 112 in U.S. territories ([**Figure 6**](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref196152243)).[198](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn198 "FEMA, Community Disaster Resilience Zones , https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/3fdfd0639ba0403e9414d05654449d32/page/Home/  .")

[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)What Role Does the Federal Government Play in Assessing Climate Change Risks to Buildings? Are There Nonfederal Initiatives?

Most building codes adopted and enforced by most SLTTs do not consider climate change risks.[200](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn200 "Government Accountability Office (GAO), Climate Change: Improved Federal Coordination Could Facilitate Use of Forward-Looking Climate Information in Design Standards, Building Codes, and Certifications , GAO-17-3, November 30, 2016, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-17-3 .") Some building codes, model building codes, guidelines, and certifications may consider some aspects of climate change. Considering climate change risks in building codes, standards, guidelines, or certifications may be challenging, because climate change risks may be based on different models that lead to different estimations of potential risks. Further, the models may not have the spatial or temporal resolution to estimate climate change risks for a particular area. In addition, estimations of climate change risks may be uncertain.

The use of consensus-based model codes and standards may not necessarily incorporate the latest editions of hazard-resistant design.[201](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn201 "For example, FEMA defines a hazard-resistant building code as a \"building code with provisions that provide a minimum level of building protection against natural hazards\" and considers a jurisdiction to be hazard resistant if it adopts either the 2015 or the 2018 edition of ICC codes without weakening provisions related to flood, hurricane wind, and seismic hazards. FEMA, Building Codes Save, 2020, p. xi and p. 3-4, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/2020-11/fema_building-code...") For example, starting with the 2015 edition, the International Code Council codes (see "[Model Building Codes](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref141975959)" section) have required at least 1 foot of freeboard be incorporated into elevation requirements.[202](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn202 "FEMA defines freeboard as an additional amount of height above the BFE used as a factor of safety in determining the level at which a structure's lowest floor must be elevated or floodproofed to be in accordance with the state or community floodplain management standards. See FEMA, Glossary, \"Freeboard,\" https://www.fema.gov/glossary/freeboard . See also FEMA, Building Codes Save, 2020, p. 1-6.") However, the 1 foot freeboard is designed with reference to the elevation of the 1% annual-chance flood, which does not allow for changes in water level associated with the potential effects from climate change and extreme events. Requirements also may exist for adding additional freeboard for critical facilities, depending on the type of facility and flood zone. Communities that use ICC codes have the option to establish a design flood elevation that exceeds the ICC code standards (e.g., to adopt a higher freeboard).[203](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn203 "Freeboard can be established as a requirement in building codes and local floodplain management regulations. See FEMA, Building Codes Save, 2020, pp. 4-4 and 4-5.")In 2016, Government Accountability Office (GAO) noted that standards developing organizations vary in whether they update the climate change risk information in design standards, model building codes, and voluntary certifications on a regular basis.[204](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn204 "GAO, Climate Change: Improved Federal Coordination Could Facilitate Use of Forward-Looking Climate Information in Design Standards, Building Codes, and Certifications , GAO-17-3, November 30, 2016, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-17-3 .") GAO recommended that federal agencies that deal with climate change coordinate with federal agencies that work with SDOs on codes and standards to help SDOs address the challenges of climate change risks in future standards. GAO called for NIST, the U.S. Global Change Research Program, and FEMA's Mitigation Framework Leadership Group to coordinate on addressing climate change issues in codes, standards, and certifications.[205](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn205 "U.S. Global Change Research Program, \"GlobalChange.gov,\" https://www.globalchange.gov/      and FEMA, \"Mitigation Framework Leadership Group (MitFLG),\" https://www.fema.gov/emergency-managers/national-preparedness/frameworks/mitigation/mitflg .") Building on earlier collaborations between the two entities, in 2023, NOAA joined with the American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE), as well as with university partners, in a multiyear effort to identify and collect climate data to inform future ASCE standards.[206](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn206 "ASCE, \"ASCE NOAA Taskforce,\" https://www.asce.org/initiatives/asce-noaa-taskforce . See also Memorandum of Understanding B etween the American Society of Civil Engineers and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration at https://www.noaa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-02/MOU_between_the_American_Society_of_Civil_Engineers_and_NOAA.pdf .") A focus of the effort is on ASCE flood resistant standards, ASCE 24 and all hazard resistant standards, ASCE 7 updates (see "[Standards](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref144125538)" section). More recently, it has been reported that in February 2025, FEMA took its name off of building code recommendations that the agency had previously submitted to the ICC.[207](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn207 "Lauren Sommer, \" Exclusive: Trump Administration Drops Work on Stronger Building Codes for Disasters , \" National Public Radio WAMU 88.5, February 20, 2025, https://www.npr.org/2025/02/20/nx-s1-5303478/fema-trump-building-codes-floods-hurricane-disasters .")

The White House, NOAA, and the Department of the Interior launched the Climate Mapping for Resilience and Adaptation (CMRA) portal in September 2022 ([**Figure 7**](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#_Ref144194128)).[208](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn208 "White House, \"Fact Sheet: Biden-Harris Administration Launches New Climate Portal to Help Communities Navigate Climate Change Impacts,\" press release, September 8, 2022, https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/08/fact-sheet-biden-harris-administration-launches-new-climate-portal-to-help-communities-navigate-climate-change-impacts/  .") The web-based tool integrates information from across the federal government, including climate maps and data, building code standards, economic justice and social vulnerability information, and federal grant funding opportunities. The CMRA tool is intended to help SLTTs understand the real-time climate-related hazards in their area, analyze projected long-term exposure to those hazards, and identify federal funds to support climate resilience projects. The CMRA tool covers five hazards: extreme heat, drought, wildfire, inland flooding, and coastal flooding. The portal's assessment tool provides hazard reports on heat, drought, and flooding down to the census tract level, including projections of future impacts in both low- and high-emissions scenarios, based on climate models used in the U.S. National Climate Assessment.[209](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn209 "Climate Mapping for Resilience and Adaptation, Getting Started with the Climate Mapping for Resilience and Adaptation Assessment Tool , https://resilience.climate.gov/pages/user-guide .") The assessment tool also integrates information from federal initiatives, including updated sea level rise data,[210](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn210 "NOAA, National Ocean Service, \" Data and Tools: 2022 Sea Level Rise Technical Report Data Files , \" https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/hazards/sealevelrise/sealevelrise-data.html .") the and the Building Code Adoption Tracking Portal.[211](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn211 "FEMA, \"Nationwide Building Code Adoption Tracking,\" https://www.fema.gov/emergency-managers/risk-management/building-science/bcat# : .")

EPA notes that Americans spend about 90% of their time indoors, and EPA provides various indoor air quality guidance documents, educational materials, networking, and funding opportunities.[216](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn216 "EPA, \"Indoor Air Quality,\" https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq .") Congress noted that various scientific studies have suggested that exposure to indoor air pollutants poses a public health risk. Congress established the Federal Interagency Committee on Indoor Air Quality (CIAQ);[217](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn217 "See S ection 402 of the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (SARA) of 1986 ( P.L. 99-499 ) . For further information on the Committee on Indoor Air Quality (CIAQ), see EPA, \" Federal Interagency Committee on Indoor Air Quality ,\" https://www.epa.gov/indoor-air-quality-iaq/federal-interagency-committee-indoor-air-quality .") the committee's mission is to coordinate federal indoor air research and facilitate the exchange of information between federal, state, and local governments and the research community, private sector, and general public.[218](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn218 "Federal agencies other than EPA have programs that affect indoor air quality, and title IV of SARA ( P.L. 99-499 ) required EPA to work with th o se agencies to address indoor air issues.") The CIAQ is cochaired by EPA, DOE, the Consumer Protection Safety Commission (CPSC), the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.

For further information, see CRS Report R47038, The Department of Energy's Appliance and Equipment Standards Program , by Martin C. Offutt .") Of note, DOE regulates energy consumption of conventional cooking products, including gas stoves,[220](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn220 "For further information on DOE's regulations on gas stoves, see CRS Insight IN12115, DOE's Regulations on Gas Stoves , by Martin C. Offutt .") The Federal Flood Risk Management Standard (FFRMS) is a flood resilience standard for federally funded projects,[223](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn223 "The Federal Flood Risk Management Standard (FFRMS) was introduced in 2015 by President Obama's Executive Order (E.O.) 13690. In August 2017, President Trump signed E.O. 13807 to streamline federal infrastructure approval. Among other actions, E.O. 13807 revoked E.O. 13690. In January 2021, President Biden revoked E.O. 13807 as part of E.O. 13990, which effect ively reinstat ed E.O. 13690, including the FFRMS. In May 2021, President Biden's E . O . 14030 confirmed that guidelines for...") which are defined as actions where federal funds are used for new construction, substantial improvement, or to address substantial damage to structures and facilities.[224](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn224 "FEMA, Guidelines for Implementing Executive Order 11988, Floodplain Management, and Executive Order 13690, Establishing a Federal Flood Risk Management Standard and a Process for Further Soliciting and Considering Stakeholder Input , October 8, 2018, p. 16, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_implementing-guidelines-EO11988-13690_10082015.pdf (hereinafter, FEMA, Guidelines for Establishing a FFRMS ). The FEMA guidelines do not require the use of the National Flood...")

The status of the FFRMS's implementation is in flux following President Trump's E.O. 14148, "Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions," on January 20, 2025, which revoked earlier executive orders reinstating and reestablishing the FFRMS.

FFRMS implementation guidelines give three methods for determining the floodplain for federally funded projects: (1) the freeboard value approach;[225](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn225 "The floodplain obtained through the freeboard value approach in the FFRMS is defined as the elevation and flood hazard area that result from adding an additional 2 feet to BFE for noncritical actions and adding an additional 3 feet to BFE for critical actions, which are defined as any activity for which even a slight chance of flooding would be too great. FEMA, Guidelines for Establishing a FFRMS , provides additional guidance to assist agencies in determining whether an action is critical.") (2) the 500-year floodplain (the 0.2%-annual-chance flood approach);[226](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn226 "The 500-year floodplain is defined as the area subject to flooding by the 0.2%-annual-chance flood.") or (3) the climate-informed science approach (CISA).[227](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn227 "Defined as the elevation and flood hazard area that result from using a climate-informed science approach that uses the best available actionable hydrologic and hydraulic data and methods that integrate current and future changes in flooding based on climate science .") During the Biden Administration, a CISA tool called the Federal Flood Standard Support Tool was developed to provide a methodology to identify if a federally funded project was in the FFRMS floodplain.[228](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn228 "National Climate Task Force Flood Resilience Interagency Working Group, Federal Flood Standard Support Tool , https://floodstandard.climate.gov/  .")

While broad FFRMS guidelines were developed in 2015, individual federal agencies took different approaches to implementing the FFRMS. Many agencies did not carry out or did not complete rulemaking on the FFRMS. Two agencies—HUD and FEMA—adopted final rules implementing the FFRMS. HUD published a final rule on the FFRMS on April 23, 2024. The final rule implements the FFRMS by updating two of HUD's regulations: Part 55, Floodplain Management and Protection of Wetlands, and Part 200, Minimum Property Standards.[229](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn229 "The update to Minimum Property Standards only applies to FHA-insured new construction within the SFHA. See HUD, \"HUD Announces Final Rule That Will Protect Communities From Flooding Events and Rising Insurance Costs,\" press release, April 22, 2024, https://www.hud.gov/press/press_releases_media_advisories/HUD_No_24_085 .") Through this final rule, HUD expanded the floodplain vertically and horizontally from the 1% annual-chance floodplain to a "FFRMS floodplain that is expanded both horizontally and vertically, based on future flood risk." The rule established a preference for (but did not require) the CISA option based on the best-available, actionable hydraulic and hydrologic data. The final rule increased the required elevation for (1) HUD-assisted new construction; (2) the standard of elevation within the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) Minimum Property Standards; (3) newly constructed and substantially improved structures within the FFMRS floodplain for HUD grants and subsidy programs; and (4) multifamily FHA-insured projects required to comply with 24 C.F.R. Part 55.[230](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn230 "HUD, \"Floodplain Management and Protection of Wetlands; Minimum Property Standards for Flood Hazard Exposure; Building to the Federal Flood Risk Management Standard,\" 89(79) Federal Register 30850-30914, April 23, 2024.") In addition, this final rule revised FHA Minimum Property Standards for one- to four-family buildings under the FHA mortgage insurance program and low-rent public housing programs to require that the lowest floor in newly constructed and substantially improved structures under these programs be built at least 2 feet above the 100-year floodplain.[231](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn231 "HUD, \"Floodplain Management and Protection of Wetlands; Minimum Property Standards for Flood Hazard Exposure; Building to the Federal Flood Risk Management Standard,\" 89 Federal Register, 30850 , https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-04-23/pdf/2024-06246.pdf .")[](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)The final rule was effective on May 23, 2024. However, in February 2025, the FHA issued a temporary waiver rescinding FFRMS elevation requirements for new single-family construction for one year.[232](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn232 "HUD, Temporary, Partial Waiver of 24 CFR § 200 .926d(c)(4) , February 20, 2025, https://www.hud.gov/sites/default/files/OCHCO/documents/Temporary_Reg_Waiver_of_MPS_flood_elevation.pdf .")

On July 11, 2024, FEMA published a final rule and updated policy that revised regulations in 44 C.F.R. Part 9,[233](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn233 "FEMA, \"Updates to Floodplain Management and Protection of Wetlands Regulations to Implement the Federal Flood Risk Management Standard\" 89(133) Federal Register 56929-57046, July 11, 2024.") and used CISA where data and methods are available and actionable.[234](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn234 "FEMA, FEMA Policy 206-24-005: Federal Flood Risk Management Standard , September 2024, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_floodplain-management_ffrms-policy_092024.pdf .") For critical actions,[235](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn235 "Critical actions are defined as any activity for which even the chance of flooding would be too great. See FEMA, FEMA Policy 206-24-005: Federal Flood Risk Management Standard , September 2024, p. 11, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_floodplain-management_ffrms-policy_092024.pdf .") the rule used the higher of the freeboard value approach or the 0.2%-annual-chance flood approach. For noncritical actions, the rule determined the FFRMS floodplain by using the lower of the [](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)freeboard value approach or the 0.2%-annual-chance flood approach. The final rule and policy were effective on September 9, 2024. For disaster-related programs (Public Assistance, Individual Assistance, the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program) this applied to disasters declared on or after September 9, 2024. For non-disaster grant programs (the Flood Mitigation Assistance Grant Program and Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities), this applied to Notices of [](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665)Funding Opportunity published on or after September 9, 2024. However, FEMA stopped implementation of the FFRMS in March 2025.[236](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47665#fn236 "FEMA, \"FEMA Eases Floodplain Requirements for Federally Funded Projects, Reducing Burden on American Communities,\" press release, March 25, 2025, https://www.fema.gov/press-release/20250325/fema-eases-floodplain-requirements-federally-funded-projects-reducing-burden .")

Lakeview Commerce Center
========================

[](https://www.thefreightway.com/site/gateway-commerce-center/)

[](https://www.thefreightway.com/site/route-3-industrial/)

![Image 6: Aerial View of Lakeview Commerce Center](https://www.thefreightway.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Lakeview-Commerce-Center-courtesy-of-STL-Freightway-lg.jpg)

Lakeview Commerce Center is located in Madison County, Illinois just 16 miles from the downtown Central Business District. Home to major companies like Amazon, Spectrum Brands, Hershey, Procter & Gamble and World Wide Technology, Lakeview Commerce Center offers tenants convenience and a skilled workforce to go along with its state-of-the-art facilities. With more than 300 acres available for lease or sale, Lakeview also boasts location within a TIF district and Enterprise Zone. The Center is located at IL Highway 111 and New Poag Road, near the intersection of Interstates 270 and 255. The I-270 & I-255 circumferential loop provides access to the entire St. Louis Metropolitan area and connects with four major interstates (I-70, I-44, I-55, and I-64) that serve the Midwest and the nation.

This page documents notable tornadoes and tornado outbreaks worldwide in 2021. Strong and destructive tornadoes form most frequently in the United States, Argentina, Brazil, Bangladesh, and Eastern India, but can occur almost anywhere under the right conditions. Tornadoes also develop occasionally in southern Canada during the Northern Hemisphere's summer and somewhat regularly at other times of the year across Europe, Asia, Argentina, Australia and New Zealand. Tornadic events are often accompanied by other forms of severe weather, including strong thunderstorms, strong winds, and hail. Worldwide, 150 tornado-related deaths were confirmed with 103 in the United States, 28 in China, six in the Czech Republic, four in Russia, three in Italy, two in India, and one each in Canada, New Zealand, Indonesia, and Turkey.
The year started well below average with the lowest amount of tornado reports through the first two months in the past 16 years and remained below-average for most of the year due to inactivity during April, June, September, and November.[1][2] Despite this, several intense outbreaks occurred in March, May, July, August, and October. The year ended on a destructive note, however, as December was incredibly active, more than doubling the previous record, which pushed 2021 above average. Additionally, 2021 had the most tornado fatalities in the United States since 2011.[3]

January[edit]
January 2 (Indonesia)[edit]
A tornado touched down in Slangit Village within the Cirebon Regency, flattening three small houses, and destroying or heavily damaging eight others. The tornado also downed several trees, some of which landed on houses and caused minor damage.[31]

EF3 damage to a home in Fultondale, Alabama.
Following a period of inactivity, the Storm Prediction Center issued a slight risk for severe weather for a broad area in northwest Alabama, northeast Mississippi, and southern Tennessee on January 25. This included a 5% risk for tornadoes.[32] Isolated to scattered severe weather occurred throughout the afternoon into the evening, including an EF0 tornado that caused some tree damage in Fayette County, Tennessee.[33][34] Later that evening, an isolated severe storm developed in Central Mississippi near I-55. The storm then tracked northeastward into Alabama, approaching the northern Birmingham metro area by 10:20 p.m. (04:20 UTC), exhibiting consistent, but broad, rotation. At 10:40 p.m. (04:40 UTC), the storm unexpectedly produced an intense and destructive tornado that struck the suburbs of Fultondale and Center Point. Significant structural damage occurred in Fultondale, with numerous homes, vehicles, and businesses being severely damaged or destroyed. A Hampton Inn sustained major structural damage, and Fultondale High School was significantly damaged as well. Considerable damage to homes and trees was also noted farther to the northeast in Center Point along the 10.4-mile (16.7 km) long damage path, which was up to 900 yards (820 m) wide. The tornado, which was rated mid-range EF3 with maximum winds of up to 150 mph (240 km/h), killed one person and injured at least 30 others.[35][36]
After no tornadic activity on January 26, two weak EF1 tornadoes touched down southwest of Tallahassee, Florida, the next day.[37][38] The second of the two tornadoes caused damage to the Tallahassee International Airport and narrowly missed the National Weather Service NEXRAD radar site at the airport, although functionality of the radar was disabled for about an hour after the tornado struck the airport grounds due to communication issues. Several planes and structures were damaged, but no injuries were reported.[39] The tornado continued east, causing additional sporadic tree and property damage before lifting after tracking for 21.4 miles (34.4 km). It was given a rating of low-end EF1 based on tree damage in the employee lot of the airport.[40]

January 26 (Turkey)[edit]
A brief, but strong F2 tornado touched down in Yildirim, Bursa Province, damaging at least 20 structures and killing one person. Industrial buildings were damaged, some significantly, and vehicles were flipped and damaged by the tornado as well, one of which was tossed onto the roof of a building. The fatality occurred when a man was struck by flying debris.[41][42]

Main article: February 13–17, 2021 North American winter storm § Tornado outbreak
On February 15, the Storm Prediction Center issued an Enhanced risk for severe weather. Multiple tornadoes, two of which were strong and destructive, struck the states of Florida, Georgia, and North Carolina. One supercell produced a tornado family of three tornadoes in the Florida Panhandle and Southwestern Georgia, with the final one being a large, strong EF2 tornado that caused major damage to homes and injured five people just outside of Damascus, Georgia. Around midnight, a destructive high-end EF3 tornado heavily damaged or destroyed dozens of homes in the Ocean Ridge Plantation subdivision near Sunset Beach, North Carolina. A community garden center and two homes were leveled at that location, one of which was swept completely away. A large metal building, several vehicles and RVs, and many trees sustained significant damage as well. Three fatalities and 10 injuries occurred as a result of this tornado. It was the deadliest tornado in Southeastern North Carolina since an F3 tornado killed eight in Riegelwood in November 2006. A total of six tornadoes were confirmed.[43][44][45]

Main article: March 2021 North American blizzard § Southern Plains 2
EF2 damage to a home north of Happy, Texas.
On the morning of March 13, the Storm Prediction Center issued a moderate risk for the Texas Panhandle, including a 15% risk for strong tornadoes.[46] Multiple tornadoes touched down across the Panhandle, mainly areas between Lubbock and Amarillo and points eastward.[47][48][49][50] A large EF2 wedge tornado moved from southwest of Happy in Swisher County to east of Canyon in Randall County, toppling a cell tower, inflicting major roof damage to homes, and snapping trees and power poles. As the tornado dissipated, a new tornado, rated EF1, formed and moved into Armstrong County, passing over Palo Duro Canyon, where several RVs were tossed and a cabin had its roof blown off. A third tornado was spawned just northeast of the second one, also crossing from Randall County to Armstrong County and lifting near Washburn, just before crossing into Carson County. Another EF2 tornado caused minor damage in Clarendon before strengthening and causing major damage to power poles and a mobile home near the Greenbelt Lake Reservoir.[51] Farther to the north, an EF2 tornado moved through a rural area near Ensign, Kansas, snapping power poles and causing damage to grain bins and pivot irrigation sprinklers, although no tornado warning was issued for the storm. Several other tornadoes touched down very briefly and received ratings of EFU because they did not cause any damage. A total of 21 tornadoes were confirmed.[52]
